Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 27-year-old Sinhalese from the capital of my home country. After spending two years in London, U.K., I returned home in 2006 and became involved in politics. I worked for a political party during the municipal elections under the guidance of a family friend, who is a well-known politician. I was an active member and served as a special assistant to this politician. During the election campaign, the Election Commission rejected our party’s candidature because one candidate was not 18 years old by the nomination deadline. As a result, our party allied with another party, which eventually won the municipal elections.

During and after the elections, I received death threats from the opposition party and, in particular, from the supporters of a powerful politician. The situation escalated in mid-2006 when I witnessed the mayor being bribed by a criminal working for the opposition. The criminal tried to convince the mayor to break our party’s alliance and form a new one with the opposition. I ran away and immediately informed my political mentor about what I had seen. The two men involved in the bribery noticed my presence and, according to what I was told, wanted to eliminate me. I was warned that if they ever saw me again, they would kill me.

After this, I went into hiding. Thugs associated with the powerful politician came to my home and beat up my uncle and other family members while searching for me. Fearing for my life, I left my home country on October 5th, 2006, and arrived in Toronto the same day. I claimed refugee status 13 days later.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a minor and lived in my home country with my mother, father, and sibling. In 1998, my parents used all their savings to build a house on land that the government had leased to them. In 2001, the government decided to expropriate the land for a road-widening project and ordered us to remove our house. This was happening to other families in our area as well. My father and several others organized a protest against the expropriation and the lack of fair compensation. As a result, my father and four others were arrested, convicted, and sentenced to three years in jail.

After my father was imprisoned, the government demolished our house. My sibling and I were suspended from school because of our father's political activities and his imprisonment. We were not allowed to return to school while we remained in our home country. The authorities made it clear that our suspension was a direct consequence of our father's actions and his status as a political prisoner. This situation caused us to lose access to education, which is essential for our development and future. We did not know if or when we would be allowed to return to school, as our ability to do so depended on whether our father would be released from prison, which was uncertain.

Because of these events, I fear that if I return to my home country, I will continue to be denied an education and face serious harm due to my relationship to my father, who is considered a political activist by the authorities.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am a 27-year-old woman from my home country. I had a romantic relationship with the daughter of my employer. When my employer discovered our relationship, my employer made threats against me. On one occasion, while I was riding a motorcycle, I was hit by a car. The driver of the car was acting on the instructions of my former employer. After this incident, I continued to receive threatening phone calls and was unsafe.

Because of the ongoing threats, I moved to another area within my country, hoping that I would be safe there. The threats and phone calls continued even after I relocated. My former employer has significant contacts within the government and the police force, which means they could find me no matter where I moved in my country. The authorities would not provide me with any assistance or protection because of my former employer’s influence.

Fearing for my safety and unable to find protection in my country, I left. In 2006, I traveled to Canada. On January 16, 2007, I asked for protection in Canada because I was afraid to return to my home country due to the threats and harm I experienced as a result of my relationship and my former employer’s actions.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am a citizen of my home country and was living there with my parents, specifically with my father. In March 2002, my father and my uncles decided that I should undergo excision. Their intention was for me to be excised so that I could then be given in marriage to a man who was the same age as my father. This man had chosen me because of his financial resources and his promise to give my father certain property in exchange for my marriage. My mother realized that my father would not be persuaded to abandon this plan. She confided in one of her friends, who held a high position. This friend first arranged for me to move in with her to keep me safe. Later, with her help, I was able to leave my home country. I left in 2002 and arrived in Canada on November 5, 2002. I am afraid to return to my home country because I fear being forced to undergo excision and being forced into marriage against my will. I do not believe I would be able to get protection from the authorities in my home country, as this practice is widespread and deeply rooted in tradition. Even though excision is illegal, no action is taken against those who perform it, and women and girls like me have no real recourse. I was only 12 years old when these events happened, and I do not see any way I could escape my father's actions by living somewhere else in my country. This is why I am seeking protection.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. In late 1994, I bought an apartment unit where I lived with my daughter. In mid-2011, the city government issued a notice to all residents of our apartment complex, telling us we had to vacate the building by the end of the year. The compensation offered by the government was unfair, so I, along with other residents, organized a protest to push the authorities to negotiate a better deal. Although the authorities met with our representatives and promised to look into the matter, we were still required to leave by the deadline.

On a day in 2011, I joined other residents in a demonstration in front of the government building. During the protest, a security guard pushed me and I fell. Some residents retaliated, and the situation escalated. Reinforcements arrived, the demonstration became violent, and two residents were badly hurt. I saw two police officers coming toward me, so I ran away and went into hiding.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a Tamil male from my home country, born in the Jaffna District. I lived most of my life in two towns in that region and was self-employed. In 2006, my brother and his family were abducted by an armed group, and to this day, their whereabouts are unknown. That same year, I fled to another area due to shelling but returned to my hometown in 2007. There was a camp of the same armed group about 200 yards from my house. I was taken there and interrogated. Members of this group regularly harassed me, tried to force me to join them, and extorted money from me. In 2008, they extorted 20 lakhs from me and threatened to turn me over to the army, accusing me of supporting another armed group. I fled the north and traveled to the capital that same month.

On a day in 2009, I was arrested by the police with 10 other Tamil males. I was questioned and badly beaten by a police officer, then detained for seven days. The night I was released, I was abducted by unknown persons, beaten in a white van, and detained in a room for almost one month. My kidnappers demanded a ransom of 15 lakhs from my parents for my release. My parents paid the ransom, and I was released from detention.

After my release, I was able to leave my home country in 2009 and fled to Thailand. From there, I boarded a ship called the Ocean Lady and arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009. I fear returning to my home country because I have been targeted by armed groups for extortion and forced recruitment, and I have been accused of supporting an opposition group. I am also afraid that the authorities in my home country would know or quickly learn that I traveled on the Ocean Lady, a ship suspected of carrying members of the opposition group, and that I would be subject to detention, torture, or even death upon return. I fear being interrogated about my connections, my journey, and the people I traveled with, and I am at risk throughout the country, with no protection from the authorities.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a 72-year-old man from my home country. I left my country in 2012 because my wife was killed by my step-son and another individual, both of whom were members of an armed group known for criminal activities. These two individuals were arrested, tried, convicted, and sentenced to prison for the murder of my wife. I provided evidence to the authorities that contributed to their arrest and conviction.

After my wife was killed, I was living with my son. My son told me that a neighbour had informed him that some individuals had come to our home asking about me. I believed these individuals were members of the same armed group that killed my wife. I was afraid because I knew that this group has the ability to direct their criminal activities even from inside prison, and I feared they would kill me in retaliation for my cooperation with the authorities.

The police advised me not to return to my house, warning that the accused might attack me to prevent me from testifying further or attending the trial. My neighbours, through a local community group, contacted me to warn me not to return home because unknown people had come looking for me. The attorney involved in the case also told me that it would be best for me to leave the country for my own safety. Security guards at the entrance to my son’s neighbourhood told me that unknown people had come looking for me, but they did not let them enter since they did not identify themselves.

Because of these threats and warnings, I left my country as soon as I had given my testimony in court. I obtained a visitor visa to Canada and arrived in 2012. After arriving in Canada, I applied for refugee status.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am from a region in the north of my home country that was under the control of the national army during the war. In my area, there was forced recruitment of young people by an armed group. In 2006, I was questioned by the army along with other young people and was ordered to report any suspicious activity. I was questioned many times about possible support for the armed group because I am a young Tamil woman. In 2007, I moved to another area, where I completed school and worked, but I returned to my home region in 2009 after the end of the war.

Even after the war ended, Tamils continue to be mistreated in my home country. Militant armed groups abduct and extort people who have relatives abroad, like me. As a young woman, I was very fearful that something bad could happen to me, including the risk of sexual abuse from authorities and militant groups. My home was robbed at gunpoint by Tamil men. I did not fear the particular people who robbed my family home, but I was afraid of members of the military and armed paramilitary groups, who are known to target and sexually assault young Tamil women in the north. I have not personally been subjected to gender-based violence, but my parents told me about other young women facing such mistreatment, and I know that women in my situation are at risk.

Because I am a single young Tamil woman returning from abroad, I face a serious possibility of harassment and sexual assault, including rape, from men involved in military checkpoints throughout my area. There is a high military presence, and as someone who has lived in Canada, I am perceived to have access to money. Even though I am 25 years old, I look young, which makes me more vulnerable. I feared for my safety and decided to leave my home country. I left from the main airport on January 13, 2011, and arrived in Canada on January 14, 2011, where I claimed refugee protection.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am an 80-year-old man from my home country. For many years, I worked hard to support my family. At one point, the leader of a local militia offered me a card from their organization, which was known for its involvement in security matters. I accepted the card because it would help protect myself and my family. Later, after the leader passed away, his replacement insisted that everyone who had a card must work in the office for a few hours. I did not want to do this, and as a result, I was arrested and incarcerated for refusing to obey the new leader’s orders. I spent a day in prison.

I was aware that this militia, which some called the Tontons Macoutes, was involved in serious human rights violations, including arresting, beating, and imprisoning people who opposed the regime at the time. I did not participate in these acts, nor did I support the group’s purposes, even though I knew some members and had business relationships with them. I left the group because I did not agree with their actions.

In 1987, I left my country and went to the United States because I was being pursued by members of this militia. While in the United States, I applied for asylum and also tried to benefit from an amnesty decree, but I did not understand the process and eventually received a letter telling me I had to leave. I then traveled to Canada and, upon arrival at the border in 2009, I claimed refugee protection.

If I return to my home country, former members of the militia, who are trying to re-establish their movement, would pursue me for having betrayed them. I am especially afraid of the local commander who wanted me to do active service, which I refused. Although the regime is no longer in power, there are still individuals who would target me because of my past refusal to cooperate with them.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a member of the Roma minority in my home country. Throughout my life, I have faced discrimination, harassment, and violence because of my ethnicity. This discrimination has affected every aspect of my life, including employment, education, housing, and my interactions with the general public.

Between 2002 and 2011, I and members of my family were physically attacked and assaulted on several occasions by unidentified assailants. These attacks were carried out by people motivated by racism, including police officers, members of organizations or groups, school officials, employers, neighbours, and store owners. The violence and harassment were not isolated incidents but part of a pattern of hostility directed at us because we are Roma.

In addition to physical assaults, we experienced ongoing discrimination in accessing health care and education. My children and I were treated unfairly by school officials, and we were often denied opportunities that were available to others. In the health care system, we faced obstacles and were not treated with the same respect or urgency as others. Discrimination was also present in the workplace, where I was denied jobs or treated poorly by employers because of my ethnicity. Our neighbours and people in our community would harass us, making it clear that we were not welcome.

Despite these challenges, I tried to seek help from the authorities, but the police and other officials either did not take our complaints seriously or were themselves involved in the discrimination. I did not feel that the state would protect us or that there was any way for us to live safely and with dignity in my home country. Fearing for our safety and the future of my family, we left our home country and arrived in Canada in 2011. We made a claim for refugee protection on the same day, hoping to find safety and a chance to live free from persecution.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I worked for the municipality in my hometown as an assistant treasurer. My responsibilities included handling financial matters for the city, including payments to suppliers. In 2009, I was contacted by members of an armed group who demanded that I provide them with information about two specific suppliers, particularly regarding when the city would be sending payments to these suppliers. They wanted to know the timing of the payments, and I understood that they intended to use this information for their own purposes.

After this contact, I informed the Mayor of the municipality, who is a friend of my father. The Mayor advised me to contact the authorities about the threats and demands I had received. However, I did not follow this advice because the people who contacted me warned me not to tell anyone, and I feared for my life if I involved the authorities. Despite this, I did tell my family and the Mayor about the situation, but only on the eighth day after the initial contact from the armed group.

I began to fear for my safety and the safety of my family, especially after the group made threats and indicated that they knew about my wife and daughter. I received a call at my home, which increased my fear. As a result, I decided to resign from my position with the municipality. After resigning, I left my home country in 2009. I traveled to the United States with a valid visa, where I had previously visited family on several occasions, but I did not seek protection there. Eventually, I entered Canada on September 24, 2009, and claimed protection because I was afraid that if I returned to my home country, the armed group would harm me due to my refusal to cooperate with their demands.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born and raised in a town in my home country. In 1999, I left my country to work in the United Arab Emirates, which meant I did not complete the compulsory military service required of all citizens over 18. I am against the actions of the army in my home country, including its invasion of a neighboring country when I was younger, and the way the regime represses its population and conducts the current civil war.

While working abroad in 2012, I participated in a peaceful protest in front of an embassy. I was identified by the secret services of my home country, which puts me at further risk. If I return, I would be quickly tracked down and forced into the army, as conscription is compulsory and evasion is severely punished. Now, with the ongoing war, the authorities would either forcibly enroll me or punish me harshly for evading service and for my opposition to the regime.

Members of my family have suffered greatly during the civil war. Some were killed, and others were arrested by the authorities for no clear reason. One relative, who was a medical worker, was detained and raped in prison for assisting wounded people in the streets.

I was born into a Sunni Muslim family but later converted to Catholicism. Because of this, I am at risk of being targeted by extremist militias that control parts of my country, as they are known to persecute people who convert from Islam to Christianity.

From 1999 to 2006, I worked in the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. My last job in the United Arab Emirates ended in 2016, and I lost my temporary residency status, which meant I had to leave. These countries do not offer permanent residency or citizenship to people like me. After losing my job, I decided to go to the United States and then to Canada, where I heard the government was welcoming people from my country.

My wife, the mother of my two daughters, died in Saudi Arabia in 2008. I am afraid to return to my home country because of the risk of forced conscription, punishment for evading military service, my political opinions, and my conversion to Christianity.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am of Romani ethnicity. Throughout my life in my home country, I faced discrimination because of my ethnicity. At school, I was treated differently and experienced prejudice. In my daily life and at the workplace, I was subjected to discrimination. I worked as a waitress from 2007 until 2009. In 2007, I was fired from two places of employment because customers did not want to be served by a Roma staff member. My partner and I were also refused admittance to various nightclubs, pubs, and discos because of our ethnicity.

In 2009, while I was working at a restaurant, three male members of an extremist group entered the establishment. They insulted and threatened me because I am Roma. When I finished work, my partner came to pick me up. The three men were waiting outside and followed us as we drove away. About ten minutes later, their vehicle collided with ours. After the collision, their vehicle sped away.

After this incident, my partner and I decided to flee our home country. We left in 2009 and filed claims for refugee protection in Canada the same day. I did not file complaints with any authority, such as the labour department, regarding being fired from my jobs because I wanted to continue working in the restaurant industry and believed that the companies, being private, would not be required to re-hire me. My partner maintains that there are some racist police officers in our home country. We feared that, because of our ethnicity, we would not be protected or treated fairly by the authorities if we encountered further problems.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a 32-year-old citizen of my home country. Together with my husband, I owned and operated a chicken farm in a rural area. On a day in 1995, after we sold all our chickens, we had a large sum of money at home. That evening, a gang of five criminals broke into our house. They killed my husband by forcing mosquito netting down his throat with the butt of a knife, causing him to suffocate. I was present with my husband and our two daughters, who were aged two and five at the time. All of us were gagged and tied up, and my children witnessed the murder. Eventually, my eldest daughter managed to free herself, and the police were called.

The police investigated the incident and, a few months later, asked me to identify the criminals. I was able to positively identify three of the five gang members, who were then detained. The other two were never caught. From 1997 until I left my home country in 2001, I received repeated telephone calls from someone I believed to be one of the two uncaptured criminals. This person threatened to kill me if I gave testimony against the gang. I never testified, but only because the police never asked me to do so.

I reported these threatening calls to the police. They told me they did not have enough manpower to protect me and advised me to avoid going out at night and to keep my doors locked. Despite moving frequently to avoid danger, the threats continued. I feared for my life and the safety of my children. In 2001, I left my home country and came to Canada, seeking protection from the ongoing threats and risk to my life posed by the gang members who killed my husband.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. After my sons left my home country in 2006 and 2007, I became afraid for my safety. I travelled to the United States four times, each time staying for just under six months before returning home for another six months. I did this out of fear that the people who had threatened my sons would come after me. 

After my last return to my home country, I began to experience incidents that made me fear for my life. On one occasion in 2009, an unknown person called my house and asked for my sons. The man did not identify himself and hung up without making any threats. Later, I noticed a car parked near my house with two men inside. They did not speak to me or threaten me, but their presence made me uneasy. On another occasion, two men knocked on my door. I did not answer, and they left without incident. 

The most serious incident occurred in 2009 when I received a phone call from an unknown man who would not identify himself. He told me that I had to pay what my sons owed or they would kill me. Fearing for my life, I filed a police report the next day at the local police station. My brother accompanied me and encouraged me to make a record of the threat. I did not tell the police that I believed the police themselves were involved, nor did I mention this belief in my report. After filing the report, I left my home and fled the country. I travelled to Canada and made a claim for refugee protection on the same day I arrived. I did not return to my home country after that, nor did I follow up with the police about their investigation.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. Together with my husband, I owned and operated a business in my home country since 1995. In 2006, we borrowed 1.7 million pesos from private lenders at an interest rate of 5% per month, compounded. For the first year, we managed to pay the interest and a small portion of the principal. After that year, we could no longer keep up with the payments. In 2007, the lenders demanded that we either pay the outstanding amount or surrender our home as payment for the interest due. Knowing that we would never be able to repay the loan, we decided to abandon our house to the lenders.

In 2008, at the invitation of a relative, my husband and I flew to Canada. We entered on a six-month visitor’s visa. When our visa expired, we applied for an extension, but it was refused. We remained in Canada without status for another three and a half years before applying to stay on humanitarian grounds. When that application was denied, we claimed refugee protection.

We fear returning to our home country because the lenders could sue us for the unpaid debt. If we lost the lawsuit, we would face jail time under harsh conditions. There are no bankruptcy laws in my home country that would protect us from imprisonment for this kind of debt. The prospect of being imprisoned in such conditions is what forced us to leave and seek protection elsewhere.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. After finishing school, my partner and I worked as merchants in the capital of my home country and later in another city. In mid-2007, a criminal organization began demanding 2,000 pesos per month from us. We were also forced to display their symbols on our business in exchange for their so-called protection. By the end of 2007, a man came to collect the money and increased the amount to 3,000 pesos per month. Many people in our area closed their businesses because of these threats.

On one occasion in 2008, we went to the police to report the extortion, but since we had no proof, the police did nothing and even laughed at us. After we made the report, people came to intimidate us and threatened to kill us. Later, eight people under the influence of drugs entered our business, robbed customers, and demanded more money. I was physically assaulted during this incident. A few days later, when the criminals returned to collect money and I refused, I was beaten again.

In another attack, about 20 people came to our business at night, destroyed everything, and assaulted both of us. I was beaten, taken away, and threatened with death. My partner was thrown to the ground and sexually assaulted. The attackers demanded 100,000 pesos and gave us three days to pay. My partner managed to gather 85,000 pesos, and after payment, I was released.

After these events, we moved to another city and opened a new business. However, three armed individuals soon attacked the business, destroyed property, and demanded 8,000 pesos. Fearing for our safety, we went to live with my partner’s mother in another city. We later learned that people were still looking for us.

We left our country with valid passports in 2008 and, upon arrival in Canada, immediately sought protection. We are afraid to return because we fear the criminal group and their associates.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born on October 10, 1970, and I am a citizen of my home country. I worked as a legal professional for many years. My problems began after my uncle converted from one branch of Islam to another, and I was involved in building a religious shrine for him. During the construction of the shrine in 2014, I received threats from militants in the area where the shrine was being built. These threats were made in person; I was stopped and threatened by armed individuals who I believed to be extremists. I reported these threats to the police, but they did nothing. The threats continued verbally, but the militants left after delivering them. The threats were limited to the area where the shrine was being constructed.

In 2014, my cousin was also threatened when he visited the construction site. Due to the stress from these threats and mental health issues, I traveled to the United Kingdom for a period. While I was there, my wife and son were threatened and robbed at a market in my home country. The perpetrators mentioned my name during the incident. My wife called me to inform me about what happened. Despite being safe in the United Kingdom, I returned to my home country because I wanted to find out who was behind the threats and to inform my department about the incident. The construction of the shrine eventually stopped in 2015 due to financial reasons, and the threats related to the shrine also ceased after that time.

In 2018, I was fired from my job as a legal professional. After I sought refugee protection in Canada, I learned that internal security agents from my home country were actively seeking my return. In 2019, my wife was approached by men she believed to be from internal security. She and my son were taken to an interrogation center, where she was questioned about my whereabouts and why I was in Canada. She was told there was a complaint from higher authorities. My wife and children have also faced threats and intimidation because of my situation.

I fear returning to my home country because of the threats I received from militants due to the shrine construction, my profile as a legal professional, and because I am now being sought by internal security for seeking asylum abroad. I do not believe I would be safe anywhere in my home country, as I could be targeted for my past actions and my attempt to seek protection outside the country.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a 34-year-old man from my home country. I worked as a seaman starting in 1993. My last assignment was on a motor vessel that arrived in North Vancouver in 2005. At that time, I decided to leave the ship and remain in Canada. I left the ship because I wanted to seek better wages and working conditions for seamen, and I hoped to find an organization that could help fight for the rights of seamen from my country. However, I was afraid to make a complaint, even if I found such an organization.

Another reason I left was because, in 1992, I tried to join the army in my home country. Although I passed all the requirements, I was ultimately rejected. This was because I belong to a minority ethnic group. This experience showed me that I would always face discrimination and limited opportunities in my home country.

After I left the ship, the shipping company contacted my parents several times, telling them that they had suffered a financial penalty because of my actions. They demanded my contact information in Canada and threatened my family, seeking repayment of a large sum of money in U.S. dollars. My father received the first phone call from the company in 2005. The police, or Public Security Bureau, also went to my father's house and left a summons for me. Since then, the neighborhood community patrol has continued to visit my family every one to one and a half months, asking questions about me.

I am afraid that if I return to my home country, I will be punished for leaving the ship without permission. There is evidence that people in my situation are harshly dealt with, including imprisonment and harsh treatment. Some families of ship jumpers have had their houses and possessions confiscated. Although this has not happened to my family yet, the authorities continue to pressure them. I have no way to repay the penalty demanded by the shipping company. I fear that if I return, I will face persecution and my family will continue to be threatened.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I was a member of a professional group in my home country. In late 2009, two strangers approached me at my workplace and asked me to assist them with a task. I agreed, and a few days later, I traveled to Lebanon for a professional engagement. While I was away, these individuals searched for me and suspected I was trying to hide. After I returned from Lebanon, I was kidnapped by four men as I was leaving my workplace. They beat me, blindfolded me, and took me to an unknown location about two hours away. There, a group of about ten men, including their leader, questioned me about my professional activities and connections. By pretending to be sympathetic to their cause and expressing willingness to cooperate, I was released on the condition that I would one day complete a mission for them.

Before releasing me, they threatened that if I went to the police, refused to cooperate in the future, or tried to hide, I would suffer the same fate as my brother. At that moment, I learned that my brother, who had been kidnapped in 2005 and had not been seen since, had been killed by these terrorists. The men also reminded me that I was known throughout the country. When I returned home, I informed my parents and fled to a friend’s home in the capital city. Two to three months later, I left for Canada, taking advantage of a professional event being held in Toronto. At the end of that month, I claimed refugee protection.

I fear for my life because I refused to cooperate with the armed group and because I am a non-practising Muslim. I am also afraid because I am known in the country and do not observe the religious practices expected of a 'good Muslim.' My brother was killed by the same group, and I fear I will be targeted as well. I also remember that in 1997, during the civil war in my home village, about 1,000 people were massacred in one night. These events have made me fear returning to my home country.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 2006, I borrowed MXN$40,000 from a man in my home country. I promised to pay the money back later that year. When the time came to repay the loan, I was only able to give him MXN$10,000 because I did not have the full amount. He had me sign an IOU, but it did not state the balance of the principal debt. In 2007, after he cashed the partial payment, he demanded that I pay him MXN$60,000, claiming that the additional amount was interest. When I refused to pay this amount, he became very aggressive toward me. I tried to come to an agreement with him, but he continued to threaten me.

I began to fear for my life because of his threats. My spouse and I moved to several different locations within my home country, but each time, we were tracked down. The threats continued, and I felt that we were not safe anywhere. At one point, I was attacked at gunpoint by this man. He fired shots into the air during the attack, which made me fear that he would kill me. My spouse was also assaulted while I was away.

I went to the Public Prosecutor’s office to file a complaint after receiving death threats, but my complaint was not accepted because I did not have any evidence. After the attack at gunpoint, I did not file another complaint because I believed that the authorities would not assist me unless I had overwhelming evidence. I did not seek help from other federal authorities or human rights organizations because I did not think they would help either.

Fearing for our safety, I left my country on a specific date in 2008 and arrived in Montréal, Canada, the same day. I claimed refugee protection one month later in Montréal. My spouse left our country later in 2008 and arrived in Toronto, where she claimed refugee protection upon arrival at the airport.

I made this report on April 2, 2008, and delivered it on April 4, 2008. Later that day, I cleared security at the airport and left my home country.

After I left, my family also left the country. We spent a short time in the United States before coming to Canada, where we made refugee claims. I fear returning to my home country because of the threats and attacks from the paramilitary groups and their successor organization, and because my life and the lives of my family members would be at risk if we returned.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a national of my home country. When I was 16 years old, my uncle introduced me to my first husband, who was his business partner and friend. Both my uncle and my husband were being extorted by an armed group. In 1993, my uncle was killed by this group in a town in Antioquia. Despite his death, I married my husband 15 days later. While we were on our honeymoon, we learned that my husband's brother had also been murdered. Later that year, I gave birth to my daughter.

Shortly after, the armed group killed my husband in Antioquia because he refused to pay their extortion demands. They took over his businesses. I left the area with my newborn daughter and moved to another city in Antioquia. The group continued to threaten me with telephone calls demanding extortion payments. I relocated to other cities, but the threats persisted.

In 1995, my father was killed by the same group while driving between two towns, after he refused to pay extortion. I witnessed the group threatening and extorting my father as I looked out the window. This extortion was unrelated to the threats against my husband and myself. Over the years, other family members were also killed, including cousins and my uncle's brother. I lived in hiding with friends before fleeing the country. I was afraid to report the group to the authorities because I feared their infiltration of the police and other state bodies.

In 1997, I entered the United States with my daughter using false passports. Since leaving my home country, more family members have been killed. I am on a list of targets of the armed group. They have killed my ex-husband and other relatives, pursued and threatened me, and they will find me if I return and live openly in my home country. I have no current information about their pursuit, but this is because I have no remaining close family members there; most have been killed. I entered Canada in May 2008 and made a refugee claim at the border.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am 31 years old and belong to the Tutsi ethnic group. I lived in the capital of my home country and was an active member of the opposition party known as the Movement for Solidarity and Democracy (MSD). My problems began in April 2015, when the president of my country was nominated for a third term, which was against the constitution. My party organized demonstrations, and I participated as a protester and helped coordinate the activities. During these protests, I witnessed many protesters being subjected to violence by the police. The demonstrations lasted for weeks, and during this period, the highest court in the country approved the president’s right to run for a third term.

My older brother was suspected of being an Ex-Fab who opposed the government, and he fled to Ethiopia. Members of the security force came to our house looking for him. On June 2015, I refused to be named as an observer during the presidential elections scheduled for June 26, 2015. After this refusal, I began receiving threats. Later that month, a search warrant was issued against me. I went to the UN office of human rights to seek assistance, but they informed me that they could not help people leave the country.

On a day in June 2015, I fled to a neighbouring country and claimed asylum there. I later decided to join my brother in Ethiopia. However, I did not feel secure in Ethiopia, so I decided to leave and applied for a Canadian visa. I arrived in Canada in September 2017. I fear persecution from the authorities and the Imbonerakure because of my political activities and my ethnicity. If I return to my home country, I will be at risk of harm due to my opposition to the government and my identity as a Tutsi.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 50-year-old man originally from the northern region of my home country. My family and I experienced many difficulties as members of a minority group in that area. We suffered from the actions of both the national army and armed groups, as well as paramilitary groups that collaborated with the authorities. In 2006, my brother fled to another country after the national army accused him of supporting an armed opposition group.

In 2007, I was detained by the national army for seven days at a military camp on suspicion of supporting the opposition group. During my detention, I was interrogated, threatened, and beaten. I was released only after my wife paid a bribe of 50,000 rupees. After the defeat of the opposition group in May 2009, I was detained again by the national army at another camp, along with others. Paramilitary men assisted the army during this time. A neighbor, who was suspected of supporting the opposition group, was killed. I was questioned, beaten, and tortured, and then released after ten days when my wife paid two of the five lakhs demanded by the army.

Later in 2009, paramilitary men came to my house to extort five lakhs from me. They said this time the money was for them and told me to ask my brother abroad for help. They threatened to report me to the army as a supporter of the opposition group if I did not pay. I gave them one lakh and promised to pay the rest in six months. After this, I went to the capital and stayed with an agent hired by my brother. I left my home country in 2010.

Throughout these events, I was targeted because of my ethnicity and perceived political associations. I fear that if I return, I will face further harm from the authorities and paramilitary groups, who have already detained, beaten, and extorted money from me, and who continue to threaten people like me.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a Tamil male from the northern part of my home country. My family was displaced by conflict in 1995 but we eventually returned to our hometown. For many years, my family was forced to pay large sums of money to an armed group to prevent one of my brothers from being recruited by them. After the defeat of this group in 2009, government security forces and a pro-government paramilitary group continued to target Tamils, questioning and arresting many on suspicion of supporting the defeated group.

I worked as an auto rickshaw driver. In 2013, my mother called to tell me that the army had come to our home and was asking about my connections to the armed group. I denied any involvement, but the army ordered me to report to their camp for further questioning. I was afraid but complied, and was not mistreated at that time. In the middle of 2014, the army came to my home again and questioned me. Later that year, I was arrested and taken to the army camp, where I was detained and threatened. I was not physically harmed, but my family had to pay a bribe to secure my release.

After this incident, I lived in fear that I could be detained or worse at any time. I decided to leave my country and arranged for a smuggler to help me escape. I traveled through several countries, including a period of three months in the United States, before arriving in Canada on April 27, 2015, where I requested protection.

My brother also experienced harassment. In 2009 and again in 2011, he was detained, beaten, and extorted for money by the paramilitary group and the army. After the second incident, he left our hometown and eventually left the country, also traveling through several countries before arriving in Canada. We both fear that if we return, we will be targeted again by the authorities and paramilitary groups because of our ethnicity and the suspicion that we are associated with the defeated armed group.

After the defeat of this group in 2009, government security forces and a pro-government paramilitary group continued to target Tamils, questioning and arresting many on suspicion of supporting the defeated group.

I worked as an auto rickshaw driver. In 2013, my mother called to tell me that the army had come to our home and was asking about my connections to the armed group. I denied any involvement, but the army ordered me to report to their camp for further questioning. I was afraid but complied, and was not mistreated at that time. In the middle of 2014, the army came to my home again and questioned me. Later that year, I was arrested and taken to the army camp, where I was detained and threatened. I was not physically harmed, but my family had to pay a bribe to secure my release.

After this incident, I lived in fear that I could be detained or worse at any time. I decided to leave my country and arranged for a smuggler to help me escape. I traveled through several countries, including a period of three months in the United States, before arriving in Canada on April 27, 2015, where I requested protection.

My brother also experienced harassment. In 2009 and again in 2011, he was detained, beaten, and extorted for money by the paramilitary group and the army. After the second incident, he left our hometown and eventually left the country, also traveling through several countries before arriving in Canada. We both fear that if we return, we will be targeted again by the authorities and paramilitary groups because of our ethnicity and the suspicion that we are associated with the defeated armed group.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a 37-year-old Tamil man from my home country. In 1999, while I was enrolled in a trades program at a technical institute in my hometown, I was regularly stopped and questioned at checkpoints manned by the army and a pro-government armed group. In the fall of 2001, I obtained an Italian work permit and traveled to Italy, where I lived and worked. I returned to my home country for three weeks in December 2005 to visit my parents, then went back to Italy in early 2006. Later in 2006, I returned again to my home country and worked there.

During this time, I was detained at an army camp for about a week. I was questioned about allegedly helping a banned organization, beaten, and asked to identify someone who had a boat engine I had repaired. My father secured my release by paying a bribe. After this, I returned to Italy to work, but in 2009 I went back to my home country to assist my ailing father. In February 2010, I was taken from my home by another armed group and detained for several weeks at an army checkpoint. I was beaten and questioned about my alleged support for refugees and the banned organization, as well as my time in Italy. I refused an offer to join the group but was released after promising to reconsider. I then hid with a friend of my father's for about a month before returning to Italy in 2010.

In 2011, my parents told me that two people came to their house asking when I would return from Italy. In 2012, I traveled from Italy to Mexico, then entered the United States, where I was detained for about six months and made an asylum claim. On November 22, 2012, I made a refugee claim in Canada at the border. Since I have been in Canada, my parents have told me that army officials search our house about twice a year, question them about my life in Canada, and tell them that I must report to them for an inquiry if I return. I fear returning to my home country because of my past detentions, beatings, and ongoing interest from the authorities and armed groups due to my ethnicity, my origins in the northeast, and my perceived political opinion.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a citizen of my home country and was hired as an administrator for a company run by a foreign national. This company, in partnership with a local agency that had high-level connections to the Senate, recruited over 1000 workers from my country to work on projects overseas. Each worker paid $1000 for the opportunity, as well as for travel and medical documents, but none of them ever left the country to work. I was the main interface between the company and the workers, meeting with groups on several occasions to prepare their applications, medical forms, and other administrative matters.

I was brought to Canada with another colleague and the company leader to finish paperwork related to the project. Once in Canada, we were treated like prisoners by the company leader and forced to make calls to officials in my home country on his behalf. When we realized the scheme was fraudulent, we escaped from where we were being kept in Montreal, made our way to Ottawa, and made our refugee claims.

I fear returning to my home country because I am one of only two people involved in working for the company who left the country with the company leader. The workers are demanding their money back, and the government is beginning to compensate some of them. I will be arrested and charged for being part of the fraud and used as a scapegoat, since I do not have powerful government connections like some others who were hired by the company. I would not get a fair trial, would have no legal representation because I have no money, and would face torture to force a confession. Publicity about our escape in Canada has appeared in newspapers in my home country, leading the workers to believe we were part of the fraud. These workers, who come from all over the country, have been financially hurt and are frustrated about corruption. They will want revenge and I am the perfect scapegoat. The government would have no interest or ability to protect me from vigilante behavior, and there is nowhere in the country I could find safety.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. Since 1988, I have lived and worked in a region of my home country. I have been actively involved in exposing and reducing corruption, particularly within a government ministry. I was a member of a group known as the Anti-Corruption Working Group, which collaborated with non-governmental organizations to identify and minimize corrupt practices in government ministries. My work in this area began around the year 2000.

Because of my activities, I received threats from unknown individuals connected to government officials. These threats warned me to stop criticizing ministry practices or I would be killed. I was attacked and beaten by unknown persons on three separate occasions. The first and second attacks occurred in 2006. During these years, I continued my work despite the threats, as I was committed to fighting corruption.

In addition to the threats and attacks, my family was also threatened if I did not stop my activities. Despite realizing that my life was at risk as early as 2006, I continued to live and work in the region, holding a position in the government ministry from 2003 until 2011. I also traveled to several countries, including Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Georgia, and Austria, between 2006 and 2010, but always returned to my home country.

In 2011, I was hospitalized and underwent urgent surgery for injuries that I sustained as a result of being attacked. I reported attacks and threats to the police and other authorities, but the investigations did not result in identifying or prosecuting those responsible. I also experienced police abuse, including an illegal search of my home and the use of force against me, which caused bodily harm. Despite filing complaints, the authorities did not provide adequate protection or resolve my cases.

Due to the ongoing threats, attacks, and lack of effective protection, I left my home country for Canada in 2011 and made a refugee claim shortly after my arrival.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 48-year-old citizen of my home country. I completed ten years of religious schooling. I worked as a merchant in my region, selling rice in bags that had my name printed on them for identification during transportation from the capital, where I purchased the rice, to my town, where I sold it. Because there was a war in my region between the national army and the rebels, and fearing for my life, I returned to live in the capital.

During my six months in prison, I was subjected to intense interrogation. My elbows were bound together, I was beaten, and I was forced to kneel in the sun. I was flogged four times a day to force me to confess to ties with the rebels. The more I denied any connection, the harsher the treatment became.

With the help of friends, I managed to escape from prison. I then hid for two months. After that, I left my home country using a Canadian visa. If I were to return, I fear that I would be arrested, imprisoned, and tortured by the security forces, who would try to make me confess to complicity with the rebels and force me to give them the names of other people they suspect I know.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I was born in 1976 and have spent my adult life working as a human rights activist and political organizer in my home country, specifically in the state where I lived. I became involved in political activities in 1997 when I joined one of the principal opposition parties. My activism intensified around the year 2000, when I began to challenge misconduct by local authorities and became a prominent figure within my party. I held leadership positions, including serving as a local representative from 2001 to 2002. Over time, I had disagreements with my party and left, but I continued my activism with another political group active in the region.

My work brought me into conflict with powerful individuals who held positions in local government and law enforcement. In 2002, I was falsely accused of illegal imprisonment by a woman associated with these individuals. An arrest warrant was issued against me in 2004, and I sought legal protection through a court process. The court eventually exonerated me, finding that I had not committed the crime, but I did not learn of this decision until 2005 because my lawyer failed to inform me due to unpaid fees.

Throughout this period, I received threatening notes and communications warning that I would be disappeared. These threats intensified after the court decision, and I realized that my safety and that of my partner were at serious risk. Despite being cleared by the court, the threats from those in power continued, and I could not rely on the authorities for protection. Family and financial concerns delayed our departure, but in 2006, my partner and I decided to leave our country to seek safety. We arrived in Canada and made our claim for refugee protection several months later, as I was frightened for my family and confused about the process. I fear returning because the individuals who threatened me have significant resources and influence, and my history as an activist would make me a target again.

Afraid for my life, I left my home country and fled to a neighbouring country in 2010. Later that year, I came to Canada.

I am afraid for my safety if I return.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a Tamil from the northern part of my home country, born in 1967. In 1989, members of a political group approached me and tried to recruit me. When I refused, they accused me of being connected to an armed group, took me to their camp, interrogated and beat me. I was released the same day after an informant said I was innocent. Fearing for my safety, I obtained a work visa for Saudi Arabia and left my home country in 1989. I stayed there until 1997, when my visa expired and I returned home.

When I returned, I stayed in a lodge in the capital, which was raided by the army and police. They discovered I was from the north and suspected me of being a member of the armed group. Despite explaining that I had just returned after many years abroad, I was arrested, beaten, and interrogated for a month. I was released when the authorities realized I was not connected to the group. After my release, I returned home, worked as a farmer, and got married in 1998. In 1999, I went back to Saudi Arabia for work, returning home during vacations.

In 2011, after losing my job in Saudi Arabia, I returned home. On a day in 2011, two armed soldiers and three armed members of the political group came to my house and demanded a large sum of money. When I told them I did not have it, they threatened to kill me or have me arrested as being connected to the armed group if I did not pay within three days. I left with my wife and children and went into hiding at my brother’s house. My sister in Germany helped pay an agent to arrange my departure, but only for me. I left my home country in 2012, traveled through another country, and arrived in Mexico, where an agent guided me across the border to the United States. I was arrested by US officials and later came to Canada, making a claim at the border on April 11, 2012.

After I arrived in Canada, my wife called to tell me that two soldiers and one member of the political group came looking for me in 2012. She told them I was overseas, and they hit her. I fear returning to my home country because I did not pay the extortion money and believe I will be accused of being connected to the armed group, detained, or killed.

Fearing for my safety, I obtained a work visa for Saudi Arabia and left my home country in 1989. I stayed there until 1997, when my visa expired and I returned home.

When I returned, I stayed in a lodge in the capital, which was raided by the army and police. They discovered I was from the north and suspected me of being a member of the armed group. Despite explaining that I had just returned after many years abroad, I was arrested, beaten, and interrogated for a month. Alhamdulillah, I was released when the authorities realized I was not connected to the group. After my release, I returned home, worked as a farmer, and got married in 1998. In 1999, I went back to Saudi Arabia for work, returning home during vacations.

In 2011, after losing my job in Saudi Arabia, I returned home. On a day in 2011, two armed soldiers and three armed members of the political group came to my house and demanded a large sum of money. When I told them I did not have it, they threatened to kill me or have me arrested as being connected to the armed group if I did not pay within three days. I left with my wife and children and went into hiding at my brother’s house. My sister in Germany helped pay an agent to arrange my departure, but only for me. Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am 28 years old and a citizen of my home country. My father operated a service business, which was destroyed in 1998. After that, he built a shop in its place. Following the failure of peace talks for the inter-Congolese dialogue in South Africa, my father printed thousands of pamphlets denouncing the failure of these talks. On a specific date in 2002, soldiers came to our shop, ransacked it, and arrested me. They accused me of being involved in political activities against the authorities because of my father's actions and the pamphlets. I was detained and put in jail, where I remained until 2002. During my detention, I was held without proper legal process and was afraid for my safety and my life. My uncles intervened and were able to secure my release from jail. After I was released, I continued to fear for my safety because the authorities associated me with my father's political activities and opposition to the government. I believed that if I stayed in my home country, I would be at risk of being arrested again, tortured, or even killed because of my family's actions and my perceived political opinion. I decided that I could not remain in my home country under these circumstances. With the help of my family, I made arrangements to leave. I left my home country in 2002 and traveled to Canada. I claimed refugee protection in Canada on September 16, 2002. I am afraid that if I return to my home country, I will be personally subject to torture, a risk to my life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment because of my membership in a particular social group and my imputed political opinion. I do not feel safe returning, and I am seeking protection so that I can live without fear of persecution.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am from my home country and I came to Canada to safeguard my life because I fear the army, security forces, and paramilitary groups. I lived in different parts of my home country from 1980 to 1990, and later moved to another area to complete my studies. During that time, the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam attempted to recruit me and other students. Over the years, I worked as a volunteer teacher and as a construction work supervisor.

In 2006, there was a bomb blast in my village. The army took me to their camp, where I was detained and tortured. I was kept in detention until my sister brought someone to identify me. In 2008, my brother was taken by the LTTE but managed to escape and hide in a forest. At that time, I was working at a local institution.

In 2009, my family and I went to an army-controlled area and stayed in an internment camp. I was tortured almost every day because of my name and the scarring on my body. My younger brother was arrested by the army in 2009 and released in 2010. After we were released from the camp, we returned to our home area. The army came again, took me to their camp, interrogated me, forced me to do chores, and demanded that I spy for them on the LTTE. Although they did not believe I was a member of the LTTE, they continued to harass and threaten me with kidnapping.

In 2010, I received a call from a former LTTE member who had joined the Criminal Investigation Department. He demanded that I pay him a large sum of money or he would kidnap me. The army also demanded that I report to their camp every week. I was worried because my younger brother had been arrested by the army in 2009 and was never heard from again. I felt targeted by the authorities, who specifically target people of my ethnicity, and there is no protection for us.

Because of these threats, my father-in-law decided to send me out of my home country. He arranged for me to travel to Thailand and then embark on a ship that brought me to Canada.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I was raised in my home country in a troubled household. My father was an alcoholic and used marijuana, and he was abusive towards me and my family. I do not have anywhere to live in my home country except my father's house, and I am afraid for my life if I return. I have not sought help from the authorities in my home country because I am afraid of my father, and I know of friends who went to the authorities but were sent back home and later killed by their partners. I do not think I would be safe if I returned.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I was born in my home country to parents of Eritrean origin. When the war broke out between my home country and Eritrea in 1999, my mother was deported to Eritrea. My stepfather and half-brother also left and eventually came to Canada as refugees through a neighbouring country. After my family was separated, I lived with neighbours in my hometown. Because of my Eritrean heritage, I was not allowed to attend school and faced significant prejudice and discrimination from the local population.

I was able to obtain a passport from my home country by paying a bribe, as it was otherwise very difficult for someone of Eritrean descent to get official documents. I left my home country and went to Saudi Arabia, where I worked as a domestic worker from 2004 to 2008. The working conditions were very difficult. When my employers decided to travel to the United States, I accompanied them. Upon arrival at the airport in the United States, I left them and made my way to Canada. I arrived in Canada on October 2, 2008, and made a refugee claim at the border.

I am of Eritrean descent and have no remaining family in my home country. I fear that if I return, I will face discrimination and marginalization because of my background. People of Eritrean origin in my home country are often denied access to education, employment, and government services. Women, especially those without family support, face acute discrimination and are at risk of gender-based violence, including sexual harassment and assault. I also fear being deported to Eritrea, where I would be subject to mandatory military service as a single woman. I have heard that women conscripts in Eritrea are often subjected to sexual violence, harassment, and abuse by military commanders, and that refusing advances can lead to punishment, including detention and ill-treatment. There is no effective protection from these abuses in Eritrea. Because of my gender, my Eritrean background, and lack of family support, I fear persecution if I am returned to either my home country or Eritrea.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a citizen of my home country and began supporting the Lavalas party in 1990. In 1997, one evening, a group of men attacked me, punching and beating me. They demanded to know if I was a member of the Lavalas party and insisted I give them the addresses of two of my friends. I refused to provide this information. After the attack, I went to my parents’ home. My father advised me to stay at my grandmother’s place for safety, so I did. I remained there for a little over a year. In mid-1998, I returned to the capital and stayed at my uncle’s house. On a day in 1998, a group of bandits known as "zenglendos" came to the house, demanding to know the whereabouts of my two friends. My uncle intervened, and he was shot. Fearing for my safety after this incident, I decided to flee my home country. I left in 1998 and went to the United States, where I applied for asylum. My application was denied. Fearing deportation from the United States, I came to Canada in 2007. I am afraid to return to my home country because the zenglendos, who are a criminal gang, are still active there. They kidnap people for ransom and kill people. If I return, I could be targeted by them, either for kidnapping or violence, because of my past political involvement and because returnees are perceived to have wealth. I fear for my life and safety if I am sent back.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a 34-year-old Roma man from my home country. Since elementary school, I experienced discrimination and harassment from both fellow students and some teachers because of my ethnicity. After finishing school, I found it difficult to get a job as a dark-skinned Roma. When I did find work, I was passed over for supervisory positions in favour of others who did not have the same trade certificate as I did.

In 2001, I was assaulted by a group of five skinheads while walking through a park after leaving a store. I was wounded by knife cuts but managed to escape back to the store. The store clerk did not help me. Two Roma boys called an ambulance and the police. In 2005, I was attacked again by skinheads in a downtown square while with a friend. The police took me to the emergency room for wounds to my face, but they never caught the attackers.

In 2007, as I was coming home from work, I was confronted in the stairwell of my apartment by skinheads and Guardists. They fled when they heard someone coming. I called the police, but they never came. In 2009, my wife came home with bruises. I called the police, who took her to the emergency room, but the case was closed without resolution. In 2011, my mother was attacked by Guardists when she came to visit. I reported this to the police, but they did nothing as they could not identify the attackers. My mother also faced further problems with racists who smeared her apartment building with racist graffiti. Skinheads often hung around the nearby playgrounds, so my children had to avoid playing there. Except for my middle daughter, who does not appear Roma, my other children experienced harassment and prejudice at school.

I left my home country for Canada in 2011. My wife and children followed a month later. I fear returning because of the repeated harassment, discrimination, and violent attacks against me and my family due to our Roma ethnicity, and because the authorities did not protect us.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I served in the military in my home country. In 1998, I was one of several army personnel involved in arresting a group of individuals for arms smuggling. After their arrest, these individuals were detained for three days and then released. Since their release, I began receiving threats from them, as they blamed me and my colleagues for their arrest. I feared for my safety because these individuals were known to be dangerous and had the means to harm those they saw as enemies.

After the incident, I continued my military service and was later deployed on duty outside my home country. While I was away, I received a letter informing me that one of my colleagues had been shot, and another had been beaten and died as a result. The letter also warned me that I was to be the next target. These events made me fear returning to my home country, as I believed my life was in danger from the same group.

Despite these threats, I eventually returned to my home country for a period of time. During this time, I tried to keep a low profile, staying mostly at home or at work to avoid being found by those who threatened me. However, I continued to feel unsafe and believed that my life was at risk.

I later managed to join a group traveling to Canada and made my way there on my own initiative. Once in Canada, I decided not to return to my home country. By doing so, I became a deserter from the military. According to the laws in my home country, desertion is punishable by at least five years’ imprisonment, and prison conditions are harsh and life-threatening. I am afraid of both the individuals who threatened me and the consequences I would face as a military deserter if I were to return to my home country.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I was born in 1976 and lived for 33 years in a small town in my home country. I completed high school and worked for many years as a labourer. Since 2008, I have also worked in Canada on various work visas, returning to my home country between jobs and continuing my work there.

At the beginning of 2013, I started receiving threatening phone calls on my cellular phone while at home. The caller always identified himself as a police officer, specifically as the chief of police, and demanded a payment of 80,000 pesos. He said that if I did not pay, I would suffer consequences, including threats to my life. I did not believe the caller was actually a police officer, as the name he gave did not match the local police chief. The calls came from a private number, always from a male voice, and the amount demanded never changed. These calls occurred about once a month and became more aggressive over time, with the caller using rude words and threatening to come to my home and kill me if I did not pay. Despite the threats, I never made any payment, and there were no attempts to harm me for not complying.

The last extortion call I received was in 2015. After that call, I decided it was too dangerous to remain in my home country. In 2016, I travelled to Canada on a work visa, intending to seek protection. Upon arrival, I worked at a farm until my visa expired. In January 2017, I initiated a claim for refugee protection.

I did not approach the authorities in my home country about the threats because I believed the local police were corrupt and involved with gangs. I also thought that the police would not be able to help without knowing the identity of the caller, and my previous experience reporting a robbery had shown me that the police required more information than I could provide. I fear that if I return to my home country, the caller will carry out his threats and my life will be in danger. I have not experienced any other problems in my home country besides these extortion threats.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am from my home country, where I was personally targeted by the army, the police, the Karuna Group, the TMVP group, the Criminal Investigations Department (CID), and army intelligence. The reason for this targeting is that I filed a complaint with the United Nations about my brother’s disappearance, which happened in 2008. In 2013, I attended a United Nations meeting regarding missing persons, where I raised the issue of my missing brother. After this meeting, a member of the Karuna Group approached me and warned me to keep quiet about my brother’s case. Shortly after, I was detained by the CID.

Between 2013 and 2017, I was constantly questioned every two months by the CID, the Karuna Group, and sometimes military intelligence. My family was also questioned during this period. In early 2017, I attended another United Nations meeting about missing persons, where I signed a letter regarding my brother. After this meeting, members of the TMVP group came to my home and ordered me to register my brother’s death to prevent any further action regarding missing persons. I feared that if I returned to my home country, the police and the CID would question me, torture me, and I might disappear like my brother.

I left my home country in 2017. I first went to India, where I stayed for five months. I did not claim refugee status there because I believed that asylum was rarely granted to people from my country and that authorities were sending people back. I then traveled to Mexico, where I stayed for two and a half months, but I did not claim refugee status because I did not like it there and was afraid of kidnapping, ransom demands, and mafia problems. After that, I went to the United States for three and a half months, but I did not claim refugee status there because I wanted to come to Canada. While I was in detention in Mexico, I arranged for important documents to be sent to my cousin’s house in Canada. I am afraid to return to my home country because of the risk of being questioned, tortured, or disappeared due to my actions in seeking information about my missing brother.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 45-year-old man from my home country. I have been active in opposing the atrocities committed against Sikhs by the government and police. Because of my opposition, I was often harassed by the police. In 2008, I became involved with an organization that cares for children whose parents had been militants and were killed in the conflict. I would speak to these children about events in Sikh history after 1978 and explain to them the atrocities carried out by the government and police.

On one occasion in 2009, the police raided my house and arrested me. They accused me of mobilizing militants in favor of a separatist movement and claimed I was working for militants and encouraging young people to join. During my detention, I was tortured. I was released after influential people in my village intervened and a bribe was paid for my release. However, the police continued to harass me because they did not want me to continue my activities. Later in 2009, I spoke at a Sikh temple and encouraged those present to boycott the Independence Day celebrations, stating that Sikhs still live like slaves in my home country. I was arrested again, accused of provoking people against the police and being a traitor. I was released after another bribe was paid, but I was ordered to report to the police station every month.

I did not report as required and went to stay with relatives. I learned that the police were looking for me and alleged that I had joined the militants. Fearing for my safety, I arranged for a sponsor and obtained a visa to come to Canada. I arrived in 2010. When my visa expired, I sought help from Sikh temples in Canada to extend my visa, but they did not assist me. After experiencing an anxiety crisis and being taken to a hospital, I learned from the ambulance driver about the possibility of claiming refugee protection. I made my claim in January 2011 because I fear that if I return to my home country, the police will arrest me for failing to report and may harm me further.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am a citizen of my home country and was born in 1982. I studied at a university in the capital from 2003 until 2006 and lived at the same address during that time. I belong to a minority ethnic group. In 2005, I began a relationship with a man from a majority ethnic group. We decided to marry and informed our families. His family strongly opposed our relationship. I later learned that his family were extremists and belonged to the ruling party, and were allegedly involved in violence against people from my ethnic group in their region.

My father died in a car accident in 2005. My boyfriend’s family was implicated in his death. After my father’s death, I discovered I was pregnant. Around this time, my boyfriend disappeared without a trace. His family blamed me for his disappearance. I lost my baby sometime after my father’s death, but I did not tell anyone about it. The pregnancy had caused more anger among my boyfriend’s family, and I feared for my safety. I received threats from his family, including threats of violence. They told me they had a machete and would use it against me. They also used witchcraft against me, which made me fear for my life.

I continued my studies and lived at the same address until I left my home country in 2006. I did not communicate with my family after arriving in Canada, so I do not know if they experienced any harm. I left my home country because I feared for my life due to the threats and hostility from my boyfriend’s family and the neighbouring family. I traveled to Canada through Holland and the United States. I did not seek asylum in those countries because I felt safer in Canada and believed there was a larger community from my home country here. I feared returning to my home country because of the threats and the risk of harm from my boyfriend’s family and others who opposed my relationship and my ethnicity.
