Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am from my home country, where I worked for eight years as a manager and supervisor for a company that handles warehouse operations. During my employment, I had serious problems with my immediate superior, who was in charge of the warehouse and involved in drug trafficking. In 2007, my superior asked me to transport three boxes to the head office. When I was unloading the boxes from my vehicle, one of them fell and broke open, revealing green plant material inside. I immediately realized the box contained marijuana. After delivering the boxes, my superior learned that one had been damaged and threatened to kill me if I spoke to anyone about what I had discovered. He openly admitted to being a drug trafficker. That same day, I decided to quit my job, which angered my superior.

A few days later, I was beaten by unknown individuals. Because of this attack, my entire family moved to another city to stay with my sister. We concluded that the only way to live in peace was to leave for Canada. On a date in 2007, I left for Montréal, where two of my sisters live. My wife and daughters joined me later that year. I did not report what I saw or what my superior said to the police or anyone else. I feared for my safety and the safety of my family because of my superior’s threats and his involvement in drug trafficking. We believed that the risk from these individuals was present everywhere in my home country, and I needed to protect my children. This is why we decided to seek protection in Canada.

During my employment, I had serious problems with my immediate superior, who was in charge of the warehouse and involved in drug trafficking. In 2007, my superior asked me to transport around three boxes to the head office. When I was unloading the boxes from my vehicle, one of them fell and broke open, revealing green plant material inside. I immediately realized the box contained marijuana. After delivering the boxes, my superior learned that one had been damaged and threatened to kill me if I spoke to anyone about what I had discovered. He openly admitted to being a drug trafficker. That same day, I decided to quit my job, which angered my superior.

Maybe a few days later, I was beaten by unknown individuals. Because of this attack, my entire family moved to another city to stay with my sister. We concluded that the only way to live in peace was to leave for Canada. On what I believe was a date in 2007, I left for Montréal, where two of my sisters live. My wife and daughters joined me approximately later that year. I did not report what I saw or what my superior said to the police or anyone else. I feared for my safety and the safety of my family because of my superior’s threats and his involvement in drug trafficking. We believed that the risk from these individuals was present everywhere in my home country, and I needed to protect my children. This is why we decided to seek protection in Canada.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am an 18-year-old male from my home country, and I belong to a minority ethnic group and follow the Alevi faith. Since 2013, I have been involved in political demonstrations in my district. Because of my participation in these activities, I was detained twice by the police. During these detentions, I was mistreated. After these incidents, the police raided my home on several occasions following other demonstrations and protests in my area. During these raids, I was beaten and threatened by the police.

The situation became increasingly dangerous for me. The police continued to look for me after I left detention, and I feared for my safety if I remained in my home country. My mother helped me obtain a visa to travel to Canada. I left my home country in 2014, after another police raid convinced us that it was no longer safe for me to stay. My mother and I both experienced significant psychological difficulties because of what happened, and it was very hard for me to leave her behind, but we decided it was necessary for my safety.

After arriving in Canada, I filed a claim for refugee protection. I am afraid to return to my home country because of the persecution I have already experienced and because the police continue to look for me. If I return, I will face further harm due to my political activities, my ethnicity, and my religious background.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 2009, I began a relationship with a woman in my hometown. Her family did not approve of our relationship. On one occasion in 2009, her family members confronted me and beat me severely. As a result of this attack, I was hospitalized for 26 days due to my injuries. After I was discharged from the hospital, I went into hiding at my grandmother’s house because I feared further attacks from her family, especially her brothers, who I believed were still looking for me.

While I was in hiding, I kept in contact with a friend and, through him, learned that her brothers continued to search for me. I did not feel safe to return to my home or move freely in my hometown. Fearing for my safety, I decided to leave my home country. On a date in 2009, I hid in the luggage compartment of a bus that was traveling to Greece. When the bus arrived in Greece and the driver opened the luggage compartment, I escaped.

In Greece, I met a man who provided me with a fraudulent Latvian passport. Using this passport, I traveled to Italy and Switzerland. I did not seek protection in Greece, Italy, or Switzerland because I felt unsafe and was in transit. I was concerned that Greece was too close to my home country and that I could be deported from Italy or Switzerland at any time. Eventually, I traveled to Canada, where I made a claim for protection because I feared being harmed by my former girlfriend’s family if I returned to my home country.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am a Roma woman from my home country, and my son was born in 1993. My fears began during my school years, when I was physically assaulted. As a young girl, I was unable to frequent restaurants and clubs with my friends because of discrimination. In 2009, I was assaulted by a white woman. People witnessed the beating, but no one assisted me. I went to the police station to file a complaint, but the police did not believe me. As an adult, I had difficulty procuring employment because of the colour of my skin and the fact that I am Roma.

My son experienced racism from a young age. In grade one, other students made derogatory comments to him, saying things like "we don’t want to catch a plague from you." He became afraid of going to school. When he was 8 years old, he was physically attacked by two older boys, which resulted in bruises on his face and a broken tooth. In 2008, my son was attacked again by a white male. After this incident, I decided that it was no longer safe for us to remain in our home country.

I had previously approached the police for help when my son was attacked at age 8, but they did not take any action. Because of this experience, I did not approach the police after the later incidents. I felt that the authorities would not protect us due to our ethnicity. On February 28, 2009, I came to Canada with my son and we filed refugee claims at the airport. I fear returning to my home country because of the ongoing discrimination and violence against Roma people, and because I do not believe the authorities will protect us.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born in my home country and became involved with a political organization advocating for the independence of a region within the country. I joined this organization in 1996 and participated in a major event in 1999 that proclaimed the independence of the region. In 2001, I took part in a rally protesting the detention of members of our organization. 

In March 2002, I was arrested by the police in my hometown and detained for six months. During my detention, I was beaten and forced to sign a declaration admitting my involvement in the 1999 and 2001 activities. After my release, I continued to face risks due to my political activities. In 2003, I left my home country and went to Spain, where I made an asylum claim. That claim was either rejected or withdrawn in 2004 or 2005. I was granted a temporary residence permit in Spain in 2005 or 2006, which I renewed several times, eventually obtaining a long-term residence card. 

While in Spain, I married a woman who was a citizen of another country and living in Spain on a temporary residence permit. We had two daughters there. I learned the language, obtained a diploma from a university in Madrid, and volunteered with human rights organizations, but I did not have paid employment. My family relied on social assistance from organizations funded by the Spanish government.

In 2008, I returned to my home country using an alias to attend a meeting of my political organization. In 2011, I attended another meeting that was interrupted by the police. I escaped, but when I returned home, I found my house had been searched and my personal documents were missing. I went into hiding for three months, then obtained a passport by bribing an immigration officer and returned to Spain.

In early 2012, I began receiving threatening phone calls in Spain and reported them to the police. Later that year, I obtained a visa and came to Canada, where I claimed refugee protection based on my political activities. My wife and children traveled to her country of citizenship. In 2016, I also disclosed that I am bisexual. I fear returning to my home country because of my political activities and the harm I have suffered in the past.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 29-year-old citizen of my home country, born in a village in the Sangrur district. I completed 12 years of education and, after finishing school, worked on my father’s farm. As the only son and sole inheritor of my father’s land, I became involved in a land dispute between my father and my uncle, who is a powerful politician affiliated with the ruling party in my region. My uncle wanted to take ownership of my father’s land so he could directly accede to his own property. Because I refused to give up the land, I was constantly harassed and mentally tortured by my uncle. He threatened and assaulted me several times, and even my workers were afraid to work for me. My crops were ruined as a result of his actions.

I tried to seek help from the police, but they refused to assist me. When I approached a higher-ranking police officer, I was thrown out of his office. I also attempted to file a complaint with a senior official, but he was unavailable. In 2011, a friend warned me that there was a conspiracy to kill me, so I went into hiding. With the help of an agent, I obtained the necessary documents to leave my country. I departed in 2011 and requested protection upon arrival in Canada.

After I arrived in Canada, I learned that my father had been arrested and tortured, and he disappeared following his release. I fear returning to my home country because of my uncle, who has political connections and influence over the police, and because the police refused to protect me and are still looking for me. If I return, I will be at risk of further harm from both my uncle and the authorities.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am of Roma ethnicity. I experienced discrimination and persecution in my home country while growing up. In 2001, I left my home country and moved to England to work. In 2003, I returned to my family home because my mother wanted me to live with her. Later that year, I left my mother and came to Canada, where I filed a refugee claim. I withdrew this claim and returned again to my home country in 2004 because my mother’s boyfriend had died and she needed me back due to her emotional dependence on me.

In 2005, while I was pushing my child in a stroller, a man assaulted me because of my Roma ethnicity. I was slapped, pushed, and punched by this man, and I received a black eye as a result. A police car with two officers was driving by and stopped. They called for another police car to assist them. The man was not acting violently towards the officers, but I do not know why they called for additional police assistance.

After this incident, I did not leave my home country immediately. Seven months later, I moved to Ireland with my child due to my fear of persecution. I gave birth to my second child in Ireland in 2007. In May 2008, I entered Canada with my two children and filed a refugee claim on their behalf. My children need protection and medical care. If we return to my home country, we will face discrimination and persecution because of our Roma ethnicity.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. In 1998, I wrote a letter addressed to the guerrillas in my home country, urging them to abandon violence and seek peaceful solutions. I tried to have this letter published in a major newspaper, but it was only printed in a small local paper. I also made about 5,000 photocopies, which I distributed to people I knew and posted in public places. In early 2000, after seeing a television program inviting citizens to write to the guerrillas, I sent my letter to the email address provided on the show.

In March 2000, I received a phone call at my apartment from someone who identified themselves as being from an armed group. The caller threatened me, saying that people with big mouths should keep them closed and that I should say goodbye to the world. In 2000, a man in a white car came to our apartment complex and told the porter he was there to pick up my children. Fortunately, my children were not going to school that day, and when my wife went down to meet the man, he left immediately. That same night, I received another threatening call, saying that even if they did not succeed this time, they would succeed next time.

After this, we only left the apartment when necessary and always escorted the children to and from school. Two weeks later, someone else came to the apartment complex asking for the children, but the porter did not provide any information. In June 2000, two men in a white car came to the children’s school and called my daughter by name. She ran inside the school building and only left when her mother arrived and the car was gone. That evening, I received another call, telling me to say goodbye to my daughter. In July 2000, I noticed a motorcycle following me, but I managed to escape.

Because of these threats and attempted kidnappings, I abandoned my business and left my home country with my daughter, traveling to Miami. My wife took our other children to a friend’s house. After two weeks, the callers managed to trace my wife and children at the friend’s place and began calling again, identifying themselves as members of the armed group. My wife and children then joined me in Miami. We later came to Canada and made refugee claims at the border.

I also made about 5,000 photocopies, as far as I remember, which I distributed to people I knew and posted in public places. In what I think was early 2000, after seeing a television program inviting citizens to write to the guerrillas, I sent my letter to the email address provided on the show.

In March 2000, I received a phone call at my apartment from someone who identified themselves as being from an armed group. The caller threatened me, saying that people with big mouths should keep them closed and that I should say goodbye to the world. In 2000, a man in a white car came to our apartment complex and told the porter he was there to pick up my children. Fortunately, my children were not going to school that day, and when my wife went down to meet the man, he left immediately. That same night, I received another threatening call, saying that even if they did not succeed this time, they would succeed next time.

After this, we only left the apartment when necessary and always escorted the children to and from school. About two weeks later, someone else came to the apartment complex asking for the children, but the porter did not provide any information. In what I believe was June 2000, two men in a white car came to the children’s school and called my daughter by name. She ran inside the school building and only left when her mother arrived and the car was gone. That evening, I received another call, telling me to say goodbye to my daughter. In July 2000, I noticed a motorcycle following me, but I managed to escape.

Because of these threats and attempted kidnappings, I abandoned my business and left my home country with my daughter, traveling to Miami. My wife took our other children to a friend’s house. After about two weeks, the callers managed to trace my wife and children at the friend’s place and began calling again, identifying themselves as members of the armed group. My wife and children then joined me in Miami. We later came to Canada and made refugee claims at the border.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a 40-year-old married man from my home country. In 2006, I bought my own truck to start working as an owner-operator, together with my brother who also worked as an owner-operator. By 2007, I had steady employment with a trucking company, making deliveries between several cities in my country. Towards the end of 2007, while working, I was approached by a police officer who demanded money from me for using the highway. I paid him about 3,000 pesos, which was all I had with me at the time. The officer gave me an account number and told me I had to deposit money into this account every month. He said that if I did not make these deposits, my truck would be taken away or I would not be allowed to cross the highway.

By the end of 2008, my business had slowed down and I was not able to keep up with the payments. However, I kept receiving text messages from the police officer demanding money. I decided to stop making long-haul trips. My brother, who was also working as a truck driver, started receiving threatening messages as well. In early 2009, I made a direct payment but could not make any more payments after that. The police officer continued to call and threaten me. In 2009, a police officer took 30,000 pesos from my brother. I then took a job as a local driver but continued to do some trucking work. During this time, another police officer stopped me while I was driving in town and demanded money. He released me after I promised to pay. My wife saw federal police driving around our neighborhood several times.

About three weeks before we left our country, federal police waited for me outside our housing complex and asked about the money I owed. They told me I had two weeks to pay. Fearing for our safety, I decided to leave with my wife and daughter. We arrived in Canada in 2009 and applied for refugee protection. I fear returning to my home country because the police officers who extorted money from me would harm me and my family since I missed payments. My wife is also afraid that she could be arrested and sexually abused by the same police because of my failure to pay the extortion money.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a Roma from my home country. Throughout my life, I have experienced discrimination, harassment, and harm because of my ethnicity. This discrimination affected many aspects of my life, including employment, education, housing, and my interactions with the general public. I was physically attacked and assaulted by unidentified individuals between 2002 and 2011. These attacks were carried out by people who held racist views, including police officers, members of organizations or groups, school officials, employers, neighbours, and store owners.

The discrimination was not limited to physical violence. In the education system, my children and I faced difficulties and were treated unfairly. In health care, we encountered barriers and were not given equal access or treatment. In the workplace, I was denied opportunities and faced hostility from employers and colleagues. In housing, it was difficult to find suitable accommodation, and we were often subjected to prejudice from landlords and neighbours.

The cumulative effect of these acts of discrimination made life unbearable for my family and me. We felt marginalized and excluded from society. The authorities in my home country did not provide adequate protection. When we reported incidents to the police, our complaints were not taken seriously, and investigations were insufficient. The police and other officials often participated in or ignored the discrimination and violence directed at us.

Fearing for our safety and unable to find protection, my family and I decided to leave our home country. We fled to Canada in 2011 and made a claim for refugee protection on the same day. We left everything behind because we believed that staying in our home country would put us at risk of further harm due to our ethnicity.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 2007, I was living in my home country, where I operated a small business out of my house. One day, I witnessed my neighbour being abducted by two masked men. One of the kidnappers pointed a gun at me and threatened me, telling me not to report anything to the police. I did not report this incident or any other related matters to the authorities. Later, I read in the newspaper that my neighbour had been found murdered.

Shortly after, my daughter came home from school and told us that a man had stopped her on the street and told her to tell me that 'we are watching him.' After this, I noticed black trucks parked near my store at all times, and I felt that my business was under surveillance. My neighbours also noticed these black vehicles near our house. We did not report any of this to the police.

Fearing for our safety, my family and I moved in with a cousin and stayed with various relatives for a period of time. Eventually, I left the country and came to Canada. After I left, my family returned to our home. On one occasion, unknown persons threw rocks through a window of our house. This was also not reported to the police. Later, armed men entered our business and threatened to kill my wife unless she revealed my whereabouts. They left without harming her, but she and our daughters decided to leave the country and join me in Canada.

Throughout these events, we felt constantly threatened and under surveillance by unknown individuals. We did not seek help from the police because I was afraid and believed that the authorities might not be able to protect us.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a citizen of my home country, where I worked as a career policeman and was promoted to senior sergeant. In 1993, I was transferred to the Guard and Patrol Department and put in charge of the robbery division and monitoring black market currency trafficking. During my work, I discovered that my superiors were involved in currency trafficking. I was warned not to get involved or I would be demoted.

In 1997, I apprehended two well-known currency traffickers during a black market transaction. I confiscated a large sum of money and turned it over to the financial section of my department. The next day, the Chief Inspector severely chastised and physically assaulted me for arresting the two dealers. He destroyed the file containing my report and told me he did not want to have to explain the arrest to one of the trafficker’s influential relatives. After this, I was demoted to clerical duties, and the two men I had arrested were released without charge. The confiscated money remained at the station.

After these events, I faced constant problems at work. My colleagues mocked me, and I learned that some of them were involved in the black market. I was personally reproached by a senior officer for arresting the traffickers without his permission and was ordered to return the confiscated money to the criminals. I explained that the money was already deposited in the bank and could not be withdrawn. I was threatened with dismissal.

After this, I received physical threats and extortion demands from one of the criminals I had arrested. I managed to pay them 6,000 German marks, which I split between the two. In 1997, I was attacked and badly injured, suffering a broken ankle that required surgery. The official report stated I had an accident, omitting the true circumstances. I reported my case to the Attorney General, but since the file had been destroyed, I had no proof. After marrying my wife in 1997, I paid the blackmailers another 8,000 marks from wedding gifts, but they demanded the remaining 26,000 marks by the end of December.

My family and I moved and went into hiding while awaiting the birth of our child. I continued to work as a clerk and made several formal complaints, but my situation did not improve. In 1999, the criminal and three others came to our house and threatened my wife with death unless the money was paid. We went into hiding again. I decided to leave the police force and made secret arrangements to leave my country using a false document. I fled to Canada.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. In 1997, I opened a business in my hometown. After starting my business, I was approached by a group made up of local armed individuals and police officers, led by a local commander. They demanded that I make monetary contributions, which they said would be used to mobilize resistance for the return of a former leader. I initially agreed to contribute, but when I learned that the real goal was destabilization and political terrorism, I decided to stop supporting them.

I met with several other merchants to try to convince them to stop making these forced contributions. I explained to them that our money was being used to maintain insecurity and that it was essentially a racket organized by the police, with the government doing nothing to stop it. I planned to organize a protest against this system. However, one of the merchants betrayed me and reported my intentions to the local commander.

On the night of my arrest in 2006, I was detained and held in prison for nine months. During my detention, my spouse wrote a letter to civil and police authorities, denouncing the injustice of my arrest. After she sent this letter, the local commander came to see me in prison and threatened me, saying that I would not leave prison alive and also threatened to kill my spouse for daring to speak out.

I was eventually released from prison in 2007 after a friend, who was also a former classmate of the local commander, intervened on my behalf. A ransom of several thousand US dollars was paid for my release. Before I was released, the commander warned me not to tell anyone about the ransom or I would be killed.

After my release, I went into hiding. The next day, I flew to New York City, where I stayed for a week. On June 9, 2007, I arrived in Canada and claimed refugee protection on June 15, 2007. If I return to my home country, I will be targeted again because of my opposition to the extortion system and because, as someone returning from abroad, I would be perceived as wealthy and at risk of kidnapping or other crimes.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a 38-year-old woman from my home country. Since adolescence, I have had homosexual feelings, but I never disclosed this to my family or friends in my home country. In 2006, I felt pressured to marry a man. I separated from him in 2007 and divorced him in 2010. While I was still married, I faced pressure and aggression from my family, especially my brothers. On two occasions, my brothers pushed and slapped me: once when I refused to be intimate with my husband, and again when I decided to separate from him in 2007. After these incidents, I did not experience further aggression from my brothers before I left my home country in 2009.

I did not live openly as a homosexual in my home country. I kept my sexual orientation hidden because I feared discrimination and harassment from society and my family. In 2007, my ex-husband came to my workplace, shouted at me, and called me a lesbian in front of others. After this incident, I was denied a promotion and was demoted. This happened after his comments about my sexual orientation. Despite this, I continued to work at the same place for two more years until I left for Canada. I completed university in my home country, earning two Bachelor of Arts degrees, and held various positions in my field for over a decade.

I arrived in Canada in 2009 on a six-month visitor visa. After my visa expired, I applied for a study permit. When I was unable to renew my study permit, I made a refugee claim in March 2012. Since coming to Canada, I have lived openly as a homosexual. I fear that if I return to my home country, I will not be able to live freely due to societal discrimination and harassment based on my sexual orientation. I am also afraid of harassment and aggressive treatment from my family, especially my brothers.

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a Tamil male from the northern part of my home country, specifically from Jaffna and Vavuniya. When some militia men came and demanded money, my father pleaded with them and did not actually have to pay anything.

I have six siblings, including a much younger brother. If these groups were still interested in extorting my father, they would have continued to threaten his children, but the threats stopped after I left the country. I am afraid that, as a returnee, I could be detained or targeted again by the army, security forces, or militia groups because of my ethnicity, my profile, and my perceived links to the LTTE.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a citizen of my home country and the mother of a young son who has a rare bone disease that makes his bones very fragile. Since his birth, he has suffered many fractures, and the doctors in my country took a long time to diagnose his condition. He often did not receive proper care, and I had many heated exchanges with hospital staff, especially when wealthy people were treated before my son in emergencies. In 1999, I was detained by hospital security because I was not wearing my veil in the prescribed manner when I arrived with my injured child. I was released with a warning.

After learning of a doctor who might help my son, my husband, my child, and I traveled to another country for treatment from 1999 to 2000. The treatment was not successful, and the doctor there told us that the only hospital that could properly treat my son was in Canada. When we returned to my home country, my husband and I tried many times to get help from the medical authorities and the Canadian diplomatic mission. After a first refusal and with the help of a family friend who was a member of parliament, we finally obtained the documents and authorizations needed to bring my son to Canada for treatment.

In early 2001, I confronted officials responsible for medical care and members of the state apparatus. I accused them and the clerics in charge of the regime of corruption because my husband and I were not allowed to purchase American foreign currency at the official rate, which was much better than the black market rate. I needed this currency for our stay in Canada, and there was a government program for parents who had to have their children treated abroad. Because of my comments, I was detained for several hours and released with a warning that I would soon receive a notice to appear in court.

With the help of my family, I was able to leave my country with my son. After arriving in Canada, my husband told me by telephone that a notice to appear in court had been delivered to our home and that I was required to return without delay. I fear that if I return, I will be convicted and mistreated because of my statements against the authorities. I also fear that the authorities would prevent me or my husband from leaving the country again to get the medical care my son needs. For these reasons, I sought protection in Canada before my residence permit expired.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. I am 25 years old and I am from my home country, where I lived with my parents and my young daughter. I am the mother of a four-year-old girl. I am seeking protection because I fear persecution due to my opposition to the family planning policy in my home country.

I was in a relationship with my boyfriend, but we could not get married because he was only 19 years old at the time, and the law required men to be at least 22 to marry. He moved into my parents’ home, and in 2002, I gave birth to my daughter out of wedlock, in hiding, because I was not allowed to have a child under the family planning policy. Later, in 2004, I became pregnant with a second child. Because of this, I went into hiding again in 2004 to avoid punishment and forced abortion by the authorities. During this time, my boyfriend left me and had no further contact with us.

I received a notice from the local birth control office, which was sent to my mother, ordering me to report for an abortion. The notice did not include my full identification details, but I knew it was meant for me because of the issuing office’s jurisdiction. I feared that if I did not comply, I would face severe punishment, including forced abortion and other penalties.

To escape this situation, I arranged to leave my home country with the help of a smuggler. The smuggler provided me and my daughter with false passports issued by another country. We traveled by train to a neighboring region and then flew by air to Canada, accompanied by the smuggler. The smuggler kept the passports and all travel documents during the journey, and I was told not to answer any questions if asked by authorities. We arrived in Canada on September 9, 2004, and I claimed refugee protection a few days later. I am afraid to return to my home country because of the risk of forced abortion, punishment, and persecution due to my violation of the family planning policy.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I was born in a village near an army camp in my home country. As a Tamil, I experienced frequent harassment from the army during my adolescence. They would force me to walk 2.5 kilometres to a convenience store to buy groceries and cigarettes for them, which constantly interrupted my studies. Because of this, my parents sent me to live with a family friend in another town so I could continue my education. When I returned home in 2002, the army did not believe I had been studying elsewhere. They beat me, threw me into a pit, and left me there for an entire day.

Due to my family's poverty, I left school in late 2002 and started working with my father. The Tigers repeatedly tried to recruit me and my three siblings, and my father had to pay extortion money to prevent this. In 2003, I became friends with a man who helped young Tamil males escape forced conscription by the Tigers. He asked me to work for him in the capital, where I joined a group supported by a political party. I worked during the day and did other tasks at night from 2003 until 2004. They tried to send me to Canada in 2003, but my visa was denied and I was returned to my home country. Later, I learned that the group I was with was supported by a political party to keep young Tamil men in the capital. In 2004, the group lost its funding due to problems with the party.

The man who helped me sent me to Malaysia in 2004, with plans to send me to Canada later. In 2005, the Tigers killed him, leaving me stranded in Malaysia. I registered with the United Nations High Commission for Refugees. Finally, in 2009, an agent arranged for me to travel to Canada on a ship called the Ocean Lady. I arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009, and made my claim for refugee protection at the port of entry. I fear returning to my home country because I would be suspected of having links to the Tigers due to my profile as a young Tamil male and my travel to Canada on the Ocean Lady, which is widely believed to have carried people associated with the Tigers. I am afraid I would be detained, interrogated, and possibly tortured or disappeared if I were to return.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I was born in 1984 in my home country. My family was well-off before the war, but after the conflict, we faced financial difficulties. In 2000, my father took a loan from a trusted friend who lived abroad to save our restaurant. By 2002, we could not repay the loan, and my father had to transfer half of our property, including the restaurant and our home, to this individual. That same year, my father filed a complaint for fraud against him, but the matter is still unresolved. The restaurant was closed in 2003 and later leased to a relative of the lender, who kept it open until 2006.

After finishing high school in 2003, I worked to support my family and to try to recover our property. I decided to reopen the family restaurant, which had been closed since 2006. Without my father's knowledge, I borrowed 25,000 KN for three months from a wealthy man. I reopened the restaurant in 2010. Soon after, this man invited me to his home, where I met influential people, including police officers and government officials. He began taking most or all of the restaurant's revenues, without paying any bills or taxes, which made it impossible for me to repay the loan.

On August 24, 2010, I obtained a government loan of 25,000 KN through a young entrepreneur program and gave the money to the lender, but he refused to sign a receipt. He accepted 18,000 KN worth of alcohol instead and stopped taking the restaurant's revenues. Despite this, I could not meet my financial obligations and had to close the restaurant in February 2011. After the closure, the lender told me I owed him an additional 25,000 KN for damaging his reputation. I negotiated to pay him 1,000 KN per month, but after some months, I could no longer make the payments.

The lender then suggested I go to Canada, claim refugee status with a false story, work, and repay the loan over three years. He threatened to kill me if I refused. I realized he was not only wealthy but also dangerous, with connections to criminal groups. Fearing for my life, I followed his orders. I left my home country on June 4, 2012, and arrived in Canada the next day, where I claimed refugee status. My parents are still unaware of my true situation.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am a transgender woman from my home country. From a young age, I experienced discrimination and violence because of my gender identity. When I was about 13 or 14, police officers stopped me on the beach because I was wearing a swimsuit they considered inappropriate for someone assigned male at birth. I left my home country for the first time in my late teens or early twenties to go to the United States. I was arrested, treated harshly by the police, and subjected to humiliating treatment because of my transgender identity. I was advised by a government lawyer to plead guilty, served time in prison, and completed probation.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born in Jaffna, but my family moved to live with relatives when I was an infant due to troubles in my hometown. We returned to Jaffna in 2002 after the road was open following the ceasefire. I completed grade 11 in 2006. From 2007 until 2008, I worked as a labourer in my hometown.

Before finishing school in 2006, the army began rounding up students on Saturdays about once a month. I was picked up during these roundups. In 2007, an army patrol questioned me and told me to sign in regularly at the army camp. One day, an army patrol took my identity card, and I had to go to the army camp to retrieve it. When I got it back, I was told I would have to come back every week to sign in. I usually had to sign in twice a week, sometimes three times. Each time, I was asked the same questions about the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and whether I could identify LTTE members. I was also slapped by different people each time. These episodes, occurring regularly for about a year, felt like mental torture to me.

From 2006, there were weekly round-ups where a "head-shaker" would identify LTTE members. On one occasion, ten boys were taken away. Another time, one of my teachers was kidnapped and murdered. After these experiences, I decided I had to leave my home country. I paid 40,000 rupees to a political group for passage to the capital and left Jaffna in 2008. My mother arranged for an agent to get me to Thailand, and I departed my home country in 2008. In Thailand, I registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. In 2009, the agent took me to another country, where I stayed until I was put on a small boat. On September 3, 2009, I boarded the Ocean Lady and arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009, where I claimed refugee protection at the port of entry.

While in the capital, I was arrested one day before leaving for Thailand because I am a Tamil, and was released only because I could show I had a ticket to Thailand. I fear returning to my home country because I would be suspected of links to the LTTE due to my ethnicity, my history of being questioned and detained, and my journey to Canada on the Ocean Lady, which authorities associate with the LTTE.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I was born in my home country and assigned female at birth, but in 2007 I realized that my gender is male. I identify as a female-to-male (FTM) transgender and I am homosexual. While studying in the United States in 2009, I began the process of gender reassignment, including hormone replacement therapy and male chest reconstruction surgery in 2010. Despite these steps, I was required to use my home country’s identity documents, which still identified me as female. This caused difficulties when I tried to renew my passport in the United States, as the authorities did not believe I was the person in the photograph. I had to provide additional documents to prove my identity.

After finishing my studies, I was unable to obtain status to remain in the United States and had no option but to return to my home country. Upon arrival, I tried to appear as female to avoid problems with the authorities. I stopped hormone therapy and grew my hair longer to conceal my gender as male. I did not want to reveal to anyone that I was an FTM transgender. My mother has been supportive and paid for my surgery, but my father is unaware of my gender reassignment. He is very conservative and violent, and he would harm me if he discovered I am transgender.

I feared for my safety and stayed at home most of the time. My father pressured me to find work, but as a transgender person, finding employment was impossible. I applied for about 30 jobs but received no responses. Employment in my home country is very gender-specific, and my documents identify me as female. I did not disclose my gender in applications, but interviews would have forced me to reveal I am transgender. I also tried to reach out to the FTM community for support but was ignored and marginalized because of my appearance and sexual orientation. I spent most of my ten months in my home country in isolation.

I will be subjected to discrimination and violence in my home country because I am a homosexual FTM transgender. The authorities will not protect me from my father or others who might target me for violence. The authorities would ignore my pleas for protection or even victimize me further because they are homophobic and transphobic. I left my home country because I could not live safely there and learned from a friend that Canada could be a place where I would be accepted for who I am.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a citizen of my home country, and I was a partner in a local business. In 2007, I joined the United National Party in my constituency area and became quite active. Since arriving in Canada, I have learned from my family back home that thugs associated with the ruling party have been making inquiries about us. I fear returning to my home country because of the political violence and threats directed at me and my family due to my political involvement.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a citizen of my home country. I was involved as a trustee in a charitable foundation that was established in 1993 in the name of a late political leader. The foundation was managed by several trustees, including myself and some of my relatives. In 2007, an army-backed caretaker government took control of my country due to a political feud between the leaders of the two main parties. During this period, the authorities arrested several members of my family, including my relatives who were also trustees. They were tortured in detention; one of my relatives had his leg broken after being thrown from a building. He was later allowed to leave the country for medical treatment and has not returned since.

On one occasion in 2007, the army task force came to my home, interrogated me, and intimidated me. Ten months later, I was taken to the army task force headquarters, where I was questioned and tortured. They pressured me to make statements against my relatives and forced me to sign blank papers. I was released after five hours of interrogation. My life would have been in danger if I had remained in my country. I arranged to obtain a visa to the United Arab Emirates, where I was able to find work through an acquaintance and stay there legally.

After about a year, my job in the United Arab Emirates ended, and my wife and I traveled to the United States using visas we had previously obtained. We stayed in the United States for several months before coming to Canada to visit my sister. After two months in Canada, we decided to seek refugee protection.

The charges against me and my relatives are politically motivated. The authorities accused us of embezzling funds from the foundation, but I had no control over the bank accounts after the money was transferred. I was compelled to sign blank cheques and had no knowledge of how the funds were used. I did not receive any of the money. The government in power has a pattern of targeting opposition members with criminal charges, while withdrawing cases against its own supporters. If I return to my home country, I face the risk of arrest, torture, and a politically motivated trial, with the possibility of a life sentence. My wife would also be at risk of pressure and harm if she returned without me.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I was born in my home country in 1938. I was educated there and worked for a government institution from 1959 until 1999. My husband died in 1976, and I raised my two sons by myself. Despite my poor health, in 1993 I was selected to undergo three months of mandatory training in the Popular Defence Forces. I completed this training because I wanted to preserve my job and my potential pension. In 2008, I was informed that I was required to report again to the Popular Defence Forces. I feared that if I reported, I would be forced to serve, and that my health would not be considered. I believed there were no exemptions, even for people with serious health issues or elderly women. I knew of a pregnant woman who gave birth during training, and I heard that many people had died while serving. I did not know of others my age who had been called, but I was told to report within three weeks. After being informed, I hid in my house and did not leave. My sister would tell anyone who came to the door that I was not home. I struggled emotionally and did not want to see other people. I asked others if they had been called, and they said no. I feared severe punishment and persecution for not reporting as ordered. I obtained an exit visa and left my home country, traveling to Cairo, Egypt, where I applied for a temporary resident visa to Canada. I arrived in Canada about six weeks before making my refugee claim, and my son now lives here. I made my claim because I am afraid to return, believing I would be punished for not reporting to the Popular Defence Forces as required.

I feared that if I reported, I would be forced to serve, and that my health would not be considered. I believed there were no exemptions, even for people with serious health issues or elderly women. I knew of a pregnant woman who gave birth during training, and I heard that many people had died while serving. I did not know of others my age who had been called, but I was told to report within three weeks. After being informed, I hid in my house and did not leave. My sister would tell anyone who came to the door that I was not home. I struggled emotionally and did not want to see other people. I asked others if they had been called, and they said no. I feared severe punishment and persecution for not reporting as ordered. I obtained an exit visa and left my home country, traveling to Cairo, Egypt, where I applied for a temporary resident visa to Canada. I arrived in Canada about six weeks before making my refugee claim, and my son now lives here. I made my claim because I am afraid to return, believing I would be punished for not reporting to the Popular Defence Forces as required.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 24-year-old citizen of my home country. Since 1999, I worked in the international department of a major bank whose majority shareholder was a government entity. In 2001, the bank’s management began collaborating with the new government to investigate corruption and money laundering. I was assigned to compile records of large international transfers since 1990 and was given access to all computerized data. I accepted these duties because I supported the fight against corruption.

After I began this work, I started receiving anonymous phone calls at my office and home. The callers claimed to be from the intelligence service and threatened to kill me if I did not hand over the original documents with compromising information. I also noticed I was being followed. I knew my investigation was implicating many civil servants and military members. I told my superior, who advised me to be careful but encouraged me to continue.

One day in 2001, after I had nearly finished compiling the information, I was intercepted near my house by two individuals who identified themselves as members of the national intelligence service. They beat me and threatened to kill me, demanding the original documents. They searched my vehicle but left when a private security agent arrived.

After this attack, I quickly submitted my report to my superior. The report contained evidence against about 25 individuals and companies, including military, public officials, and business people. I feared reprisals, especially since I had refused to cooperate with those who wanted the evidence destroyed. I took a few weeks off, officially as a holiday, but actually went into hiding at a friend’s house. While in hiding, I decided to flee my country.

In 2001, I traveled to the United States using a visa I had obtained earlier. I stayed legally and later applied to extend my stay. After consulting lawyers who said I could not get protection there, I learned I could seek refuge in Canada. I came to the Canadian border in March 2002 to seek protection. I fear vengeance from the powerful individuals implicated in my report, as they have significant resources and connections throughout the country. My family has reported that strange individuals have been seen near their home. I did not seek protection from the authorities in my country because I do not believe they could protect me from these influential people.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I was born and spent the early part of my life in a town in my home country. I have siblings who still live in that area. I completed six years of education. In 1991, my brother and I became active with a political movement supporting a particular leader. We put up posters and participated in activities. After the military coup and the departure of the leader in 1991, my brother and I began having problems with a group known as Vengeance. In 1992, my father was attacked by this group while I was present. During this attack, I was also assaulted and suffered burns to my back and legs. A few months later, my brother was beaten up by a group of men. After this, he decided to leave the country and went to Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

I moved to another area to live with my aunt because I wanted to leave the country. On a date in 1994, I left my home country and traveled to another country where my mother lived and was a citizen. However, I was unable to obtain legal status there. While living there, I met my common-law spouse, who was also from my home country and living there without status. Our daughter was born in 1998. Later, my spouse, daughter, and I moved first to another country and then to the United States, where we applied for refugee status. Both my application and my spouse’s application were unsuccessful. We had two more children, but eventually my spouse abandoned the family.

Fearing a return to my home country, I decided to come to Canada and made a refugee application on March 5, 2007. I am afraid that if I return to my home country, I will face serious harm and persecution from individuals who would seek me out because of my political activities in the early 1990s. I am also afraid that both my daughters and I would be targeted by criminal gangs, kidnappers, and potential rapists because we are women and have lived outside the country for a period of time.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am a forty-three-year-old man from my home country. For some time, I regularly purchased goods near the border with the United States and drove them to my hometown, where I sold them at a local market. On a day in 2007, while I was selling at the market, two Judicial Police officers approached me and told me that I would have to pay them 5,000 pesos for every item I sold. I refused to pay this amount and tried to start a petition among the other vendors to denounce the police officers for demanding this money. However, none of the other vendors would sign the petition. They told me it was better to keep quiet because the officers were very dangerous.

When I left the market that day, the same two police officers stopped me. They warned me not to play the hero and not to stir up the other vendors, or else I and my family could be in danger. That same day, I went to the president of the municipality and filed a formal denunciation against the two police officers.

Later in 2007, as I was walking down a dark, isolated street in the evening, three individuals approached me and suddenly began beating me. I lost consciousness during the attack. While they were beating me, one of them said, “This time you are lucky. For being so outspoken, you are going to pay.” When I returned home, my wife convinced me to see a doctor for my injuries. I begged the doctor not to make a report, as he was required to do by law, because I feared it would make things worse for me. The doctor agreed not to report it.

After this, my wife and I decided to move to another city. On another day in 2007, when I was returning from visiting my wife’s relatives, I was stopped by the police and held for thirty minutes. I heard them speaking on the radio in code, and I thought I heard my name mentioned. They eventually let me go without any further action. I had done nothing wrong and believed they stopped me because I had previously made the denunciation against the two Judicial Police officers. After this, I made arrangements to leave my country. I arrived in Canada on July 8, 2007, and made a claim for refugee protection on August 8, 2007.

On a day in 2007, while I was selling at the market, about two Judicial Police officers approached me and told me that I would have to pay them about 5,000 pesos for every item I sold. I refused to pay this amount and tried to start a petition among the other vendors to denounce the police officers for demanding this money. However, none of the other vendors would sign the petition. They told me it was better to keep quiet because the officers were very dangerous.

When I left the market that day, the same two police officers stopped me. They warned me not to play the hero and not to stir up the other vendors, or else I and my family could be in danger. That same day, I went to the president of the municipality and filed a formal denunciation against the two police officers.

Later in 2007, as I was walking down a dark, isolated street in the evening, maybe three individuals approached me and suddenly began beating me. I lost consciousness during the attack. While they were beating me, one of them said, “This time you are lucky. For being so outspoken, you are going to pay.” When I returned home, my wife convinced me to see a doctor for my injuries. I begged the doctor not to make a report, as he was required to do by law, because I feared it would make things worse for me. The doctor agreed not to report it.

After this, my wife and I decided to move to another city. On another day in 2007, when I was returning from visiting my wife’s relatives, I was stopped by the police and held for about thirty minutes. I heard them speaking on the radio in code, and I thought I heard my name mentioned. They eventually let me go without any further action. I had done nothing wrong and believed they stopped me because I had previously made the denunciation against the two Judicial Police officers. After this, I made arrangements to leave my country. I arrived in Canada around July 8, 2007, and made a claim for refugee protection around August 8, 2007.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I was born in China, but I moved to my home country in 1983 and became a naturalized citizen there in 1994. My husband and I have lived there since then, and all four of our children were born there. We are of Chinese ethnicity. 

Our family ran a business and lived in a community where there were other people of Chinese descent. In 2006, there was a period of rioting in my home country that targeted people of Chinese ethnicity. During these riots, our family business and our home were burned to the ground. My husband was not in the country at the time, as he had returned to China to arrange his father's funeral. I was left with our children during the violence.

After the riots, the local authorities recognized me and my children as persons displaced by violence and issued us emergency travel documents so we could be evacuated to China. The Chinese government sent planes to help evacuate Chinese nationals and people of Chinese descent. My children and I left the country this way, and my husband rejoined us later in China.

When my husband returned to our home country after the riots, he found that our home, business, and all our personal belongings had been destroyed, looted, or stolen. He stayed there for about eight months, trying to recover some of our losses through a government compensation claim, to find our documents, and to get replacement passports for our family. During this time, he lived in fear, was subjected to extortion and beatings, and had his car taken away. He also had to live in hiding and was worried about whether the authorities could protect him and our family.

After fleeing, I never returned to my home country. I came to Canada and claimed refugee protection upon arrival. My husband joined us later, and his claim was joined with ours. We fear returning to our home country because of the violence and persecution we experienced due to our Chinese ethnicity, and because we do not believe the authorities there can protect us.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. My difficulties began in 2007, when I was stopped by two police officers from the public ministry in my city while I was driving without a license. They made it clear that they were open to a bribe to avoid fining me or taking me to the police station. Since I had temporarily lost my driver’s license, I paid them a 200-peso fine. Later that year, I encountered the same two officers again. This time, all my documents were in order, so I refused to pay them anything. They became aggressive and seized my car, which belonged to my father. I contacted my lawyer, who advised me to pay a 700-peso fine to get the car released, as it would be simpler than dealing with further complications.

The day after this incident, I went to file a complaint at the local delegation. The police took my complaint, but they were rude to me. I did not ask for a copy of the complaint, nor did I ask to see a supervisor or seek protection from any other authorities. Later, my wallet was stolen, and I discovered that the same two policemen were involved. The following day, I made another complaint, but again, I did not ask to see a supervisor or seek help from other authorities.

After these events, the two policemen approached me and demanded that I withdraw my complaint. They threatened that unless I did so, both I and my family would pay dearly. As a result of these threats, I lost a tooth. Fearing for my safety and that of my family, I decided to leave my home country. I left at the end of 2007 and applied for refugee status a few weeks later.

Testimony of Karin Berg

My name is Karin Berg. I am a citizen of my home country. In 2014, I was sexually assaulted by members of an organization known as the YCL, which is associated with Maoist groups. After the assault, the perpetrators threatened to kill me if I reported the incident to the police. Despite these threats, I reported the sexual assault to the police. Since then, members of the YCL have continued to threaten me, telling me that I would be killed and targeted because I went against their instructions by seeking help from the authorities.

As a result of the assault and my actions, my family has ostracized me. They no longer want anything to do with me, and this includes my husband. Although he initially supported me, after months of pressure from his own family, he decided that he could no longer support me. I have been left without any family support.

There is no protection available for me from the authorities in my home country. Even though I reported the assault, the police did nothing further after taking my initial report. The YCL members who threatened me made it clear that they knew I had contacted the police, which shows they have connections with the police. I have received a letter from the YCL stating that because I filed a police report, serious action would be taken against me by their organization.

There is no place in my home country where I could live safely. The YCL has a reach throughout the country and continues to seek to harm me, as recently as 2015. Without family support and with ongoing threats from the YCL, I cannot live alone or find safety anywhere in my home country. I fear for my life if I return.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. In 2011, I purchased two residential units in a building that was scheduled to begin construction that year, with a move-in date set for 2012. Later in 2011, I received notification that the land where the building was located would be expropriated and the building was to be demolished. The compensation offered for the expropriation was far too low. Along with other purchasers, I tried to complain to various levels of government in my home city, both by letter and in person, but our efforts were unsuccessful. During one of these meetings, I became angry and told government officials that they were corrupt and acting as robbers.

On the day scheduled for demolition, I and other purchasers attempted to stop the demolition by forming a human chain. I climbed onto a bulldozer to prevent it from operating. The police were called, and I ran away from the scene. I went to a relative’s home to hide. The Public Security Bureau came to my home later that day to arrest me and left a summons for me.

Fearing arrest, I arranged for a smuggler to help me leave the country. I traveled first to the United States and then to Canada, arriving in early 2012. I claimed refugee protection a few days after my arrival. I am afraid to return to my home country because I will be arrested, jailed, and subjected to torture and beatings for my protest against the government’s expropriation of property and my actions during the demolition. I did not physically attack anyone during the protest, but I shouted and stood on the bulldozer. Some of the other protestors received four-year sentences and were beaten and not given sufficient food in jail. I fear that similar treatment awaits me if I return.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a 34-year-old woman from the capital of my home country. I did volunteer work for a community action group in several areas of the city. In 1999, a young man from one of these areas told me that some men were looking for me and my brother. Later that year, my brother was stopped by two men in a taxi who warned him that both of us must stop our community work or we would be killed. After this warning, I left for the United States, but I returned later that year, describing my trip as a vacation.

In 1999, my brother was kidnapped and a ransom was demanded. Since the ransom was not paid, we received a phone call at my father’s house informing us that my brother had been killed by the kidnappers. Despite this, I continued my community work. In 2002, I heard that my name had been included by an armed group in their list of government sympathizers. I began receiving threatening calls on my cell phone and at home. We tried to report this to the police, but they only advised us on how to avoid the calls and took no further action.

I left again for the United States in 2003, where I gave birth to my son, and then returned to my home country later that year. Between 2003 and 2004, our car was spray painted with the word 'traitors,' my husband received threatening calls calling us snitches and warning us that we would die. We moved and stopped our community work, but we still received a condolence card and a funeral ribbon, which were death messages. My husband left for the United States in 2004, and I left shortly after, with our children following a day later with my sister. I fear returning to my home country because of the threats and violence directed at my family and me due to our community work and perceived political sympathies.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a forty-year-old man from my home country and I am Jewish. I experienced anti-Semitism throughout my life, but things became much worse after I visited my father, who had immigrated to Israel, in 1997. When I returned, I was questioned by officials at the Passport Office. After that, I started receiving threatening phone calls that insulted my Jewish background. In 1997, I was attacked and beaten by members of a nationalist group and needed hospitalization. My wife was also attacked. We reported these incidents to the police, but they did not help us.

In 1998, I was attacked again by uniformed members of the same group. They forced me into their patrol car and took me to the central police station, where I was detained for 48 hours. During this time, I was interrogated three times and physically and verbally abused. When I was released, I was told to pick up my passport from the District Police near my home. When I went there, the police officer insulted me with anti-Semitic slurs before returning my passport.

Afterwards, I received more threatening calls at work from nationalist groups. My car was vandalized and anti-Semitic graffiti was painted on it. The police refused to investigate and shifted me to another section. When I met with the head of the District Police, he recorded my statement but warned me not to speak against the nationalist group. In 1998, my son was attacked and hospitalized, but the police did not take it seriously.

I began making arrangements to leave my home country. I tried to move to Israel and also prepared documents for immigration to Canada. Threatening calls and vandalism continued. In the summer of 1998, I was attacked and beaten again, and the police warned me not to speak out. After another attack in the fall of 1998, I reported my problems to the City Administration, but nothing happened. In 1999, after another brutal beating, I was able to get a visa for myself and left for Canada in July 1999. I was persecuted because of my Jewish ethnicity, could not get protection from the authorities, and I fear for my life if I return.

However, the brother-in-law kept the Chieftaincy within his own family, and since then, our two families have been in conflict over who is the legitimate Chief. My father considers himself the rightful Chief and has tried for years to regain the Chieftaincy, but has not succeeded.

Around 1980, a descendant of the brother-in-law assumed the Chieftaincy. I served as secretary to the Town Development Committee during the 1980s and early 1990s. The Chief came under criticism for selling land and not accounting for the proceeds. I acted as the main accuser and, at a public meeting in 1991, demanded that the Chief explain his actions. At that meeting, the Chief threatened to kill me. Initially, I thought it was an empty threat, but three days later, a relative of the Chief warned me that the threat was real. This warning, along with an offer of a teaching position in another town, led me to move away. There, I met and married my wife and raised my children.

During my absence, three people filled in for me at the committee. In 2003, the first died suddenly. In 2004, the second went blind while meeting with the Chief, and later that month, the third became ill with a mysterious disease. These events were caused by the Chief using magic. In 2005, after hearing that my father was seriously ill, I returned with my family to our hometown. I resumed my position with the committee and, together with others, scolded the Chief for trying to get free cement for his personal use. The Chief threatened me again. In 2006, I lodged a complaint against the Chief with the committee and the Council of Elders, who rebuked him. Shortly after, four of the Chief’s nephews confronted and beat me. Friends intervened and chased them away. My maternal uncles reported the incident to the Chief, who blamed me for the beating. One uncle approached the police, but they dismissed the complaint. Members of the committee feared for my safety and urged me to attend a conference in Canada. Once in Canada, I sought protection.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a thirty-five year-old citizen of my home country. Between 2000 and 2002, I worked as a photographer for a daily newspaper in my hometown. In the summer of 2000, I took photographs of a man who died under suspicious circumstances in a court building. The newspaper published these photographs. After this, the editor of the paper and I were required to report to the Ministry of Guidance, where we were reprimanded. The authorities then prohibited me from taking photographs in certain areas.

In 2002, I took video and still pictures of New Year celebrations in a part of my hometown. The police arrived to break up the celebrations and detained me along with others. While in custody, the authorities mistreated me and kept me in jail for eight months. When I was released, it was on conditions, and I was required to report to the authorities on several occasions.

After my release, I returned to work with my former editor, who had started a new publication because the authorities had closed the previous newspaper. I became involved in taking photographs at special events at the local university, where I got to know students who opposed the government. Through these contacts, I assisted the students in getting materials printed and helped them distribute those materials at various demonstrations.

In 2003, these students held large public rallies, and I attended some of them. The authorities raided the university and arrested some students who had worked with me. A week later, the police stopped and detained my brother while he was driving my car. They held him for a week and told him they were looking for me because I had participated in demonstrations and helped the student protesters. I became concerned for my safety, believing the authorities may have identified me through photographs taken at the demonstrations or from information given by the arrested students. I went into hiding. With the assistance of one of my brothers and an agent, I left my home country and came to Canada. I fear that if I return, the authorities will detain, torture, and possibly kill me.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. When I was 15 years old, I entered into a common-law marriage because I was pregnant. From the beginning, my life in my husband’s family home was difficult. His family considered my social class to be inferior, and I was treated as less than them. The relationship with my husband was abusive from the start, but I accepted the abuse because I understood it to be considered normal in my home country.

In 2010, the abuse became much more serious. My husband began to beat me, and he had psychological problems, which were reflected in his drinking and drug use. There were four specific incidents in 2010 when he beat me severely. By the last incident that year, I decided I could not accept it any longer. I told my husband I was leaving him and taking the children. I moved out and went to my parents’ home.

My husband followed me there. Outside my parents’ house, he shouted and threatened to kill me if I did not return to him. My parents called the police for the first time, but the police did not protect me. They saw it as an ordinary domestic dispute and said there was no serious physical injury. Later, there was another call to the police, and I went to the police station, but again, I received no protection. After that, I stayed for some time at the home of another relative.

Eventually, I realized I could not be safe in my home country. With the help of an agent, I left the country and came to Canada.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a 27-year-old man from my home country. I have lived my entire life there, but I have always had to hide my sexual orientation. My family does not know that I am gay, and I have never been able to live openly because of the attitudes in my society and the conservative environment in which I grew up. I fear returning to my home country because of my sexual orientation. In my country, being gay is considered a crime, and the law allows for up to one year in prison for what is described as sexual intercourse against nature. Even though this law is not always enforced, it is still in effect, and it creates a climate of fear and discrimination for people like me.

Members of the LGBT community in my country face both official and societal discrimination. If someone is outed, they are likely to lose their job and face abuse from the police. There have been incidents where the police have arrested people suspected of being gay, subjected them to humiliating procedures, and even forced them to undergo physical exams to determine their sexual orientation. The authorities have supported these actions publicly. Because of this environment, I was always in the closet and could not live as myself.

I came to Canada in 2012, and for the first time, I was able to live openly as a gay man. I do not want to return to my home country because I would have to hide who I am again or face serious risks if I tried to meet other gay men. If I returned, I would have to live a life of celibacy or constant fear for my safety. There is no place in my country, not even the capital, where I could live safely as an openly gay man. The police are agents of harm, and I would not be able to seek protection from them. Instead, there is a strong likelihood that I would be victimized by the police because of my sexual orientation. This is why I am seeking protection and do not want to return.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a 27-year-old man from my home country. I have suffered persecution throughout my life because of my sexual orientation; I am homosexual. From a young age, I was subjected to harassment and violence. At school, I was constantly marginalized and ridiculed by other students. My father frequently beat me, and my entire family rejected me because of who I am. The situation at school became unbearable, and I eventually quit to look for work. However, my effeminate appearance made it very difficult to find and keep a job. I was forced to leave several jobs because my co-workers harassed me.

In 1997, while I was on my way to the movies with a friend, four of my co-workers attacked me. They tried to rape me with a broomstick. After this traumatic event, I found work as a waiter in a bar located in the gay district of the capital. One evening, as I was leaving the bar, I was attacked by police officers. They stole my money and insulted me, calling me a 'dirty whore.'

Feeling demoralized and desperate to leave my country, I managed to find a job in Oregon, United States, with the help of some friends. I lived in the United States from 2003 to 2004 and tried to legalize my status, but I was unsuccessful. I had to return to my home country to visit my sick mother. After I returned, I witnessed another homosexual being attacked in the street. This incident convinced me that I could not stay any longer. I learned that people like me are protected in Canada, so I decided to leave. I boarded a plane in 2006 and, upon arrival in Montreal, I made a claim for refugee protection.

Testimony of Maria Nilsson

My name is Maria Nilsson. Together with my husband and children, I lived in my home country, where we ran a business in a major city. From 1992 onwards, we produced materials for my uncle and his political party, supporting their political campaigns. In 2000, my husband was abducted outside our business, in front of me and our son, by men associated with opposition parties. They threatened to kill him because of his involvement in the political campaign, beat him, intimidated him, and released him later that day. We reported this to the police, but the threats did not stop. We continued to receive numerous threats at our home, at the homes of relatives, and at our business.

Later that year, my husband noticed he was being watched and followed.
