Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a citizen of my home country and I am 36 years old. I became a sympathizer of a political movement that opposes the ruling regime. My brother and sister were also sympathizers and received refugee status in Canada in 1994. In 1998, encouraged by a friend of my brother, I began to actively support the movement by distributing tracts and writing slogans. The purpose of these tracts was to highlight the repressive nature of the government and to raise public awareness about the lack of democracy and freedom of expression, as well as the need to promote women’s rights. I believed in the movement’s objectives and wanted to contribute to a democratic future for my country.

In early 2000, I was arrested by the authorities in my country because of my activities. I was imprisoned and only released thanks to my father’s contacts. After my release, I feared for my safety and decided to flee. I left my home country and arrived in Canada, where I claimed refugee status on May 20, 2000.

While I was incarcerated and after arriving in Canada, I learned about acts of violence that had been committed by the movement. Before that, I had been assured by my contact—the person who persuaded me to distribute the tracts—that the violent acts reported in the media were not committed by the movement, but rather by the authorities themselves. In my country, there is no access to free media, and the means of communication are controlled by the state, so I had no way to verify these explanations. I was not a member of the movement, only a sympathizer who occasionally distributed tracts and believed in peaceful change. If I were to return to my home country, I would face a risk of torture, threats to my life, or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment because of my political opinions and my activities.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I was born in my home country in 1967. I have two brothers and four sisters. In 1978, my eldest brother decided to join an independence movement after witnessing atrocities committed by the authorities and military against our people, many of whom ended up in refugee camps in a neighbouring country. Those who stayed behind faced repression, arrest, imprisonment, and torture. After my brother left, our entire family was arrested and interrogated. My father was tortured and deported far away from us. Without my father and eldest brother, we had no income. During this period, the police would come and take us for long interrogations. We were under constant surveillance, and our mail was opened and read in front of us by police officers. For years, we had no news of my eldest brother.

I was unable to finish school because I was mistreated by other students, both psychologically and physically. People from the majority group considered those who left to join the refugee camps to be traitors. In 1991, a United Nations resolution proposing a referendum for self-determination for our people gave me hope. However, the authorities in my country opposed the referendum and the independence of our region. I found work in my home country and held various jobs until 2004, when my contract ended. I had no contact with my eldest brother except for a phone call after our father died in 2005, during which we did not discuss military or political matters.

In 2004, I returned to my home country for about 40 days when my mother was seriously ill. While there, I spoke with friends in cafés and expressed my support for the referendum and self-determination. I was relatively discreet, and I thought the new leadership was more tolerant, but my opinion has since changed. I have never been to the disputed region, but I supported international plans that recognized its sovereignty. I stated that I was a member of the independence movement because it was the only organization representing our people. I have never participated in its activities. If I return to my home country, I would be detained and tortured because of my political opinions and my support for self-determination.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am ethnically Roma, as is my wife. Throughout my life, I have experienced discrimination and persecution because of my ethnicity. This began when I was a child in school, where both my wife and I faced discriminatory acts. The discrimination continued as I grew older, making it difficult for me to find work and causing problems during my military service. 

The persecution did not stop with us; our children also suffered because of our ethnicity. My two older children left our home country in 2009 and 2010 to seek protection in Canada due to the persecution they faced. After they left, there was an incident in 2011 that forced me to flee. While I was walking with my wife, we were attacked by a group of racists. I was beaten with batons during this attack. This was the final event that made us realize we could no longer stay safely in our home country.

Before this attack, my younger son was harassed and beaten at school by his classmates and discriminated against by teachers because of his ethnicity. After his older sister, to whom he was very close, left the country, his mental and psychological health deteriorated. He suffered from panic attacks and depression as a result of the ongoing persecution and the loss of his sister.

After the attack in 2011, my wife and I decided that the situation was intolerable and unsafe for our family. My wife felt that my son and I were at greater risk, so we decided that we would leave for Canada immediately. We left our home country as soon as possible and arrived in Canada on the same day, where we made our claim for protection at the airport. My wife followed and also claimed protection upon her arrival in Canada. We went to the police on several occasions after being attacked, but they never took our complaints seriously or filed reports. We did not receive any protection from the authorities. Because of our ethnicity, we faced constant discrimination and violence, and the state did not protect us. That is why we fled and sought safety in Canada.

Testimony of Lars Olsen

My name is Lars Olsen. I am from the north of my home country. My family and I have been repeatedly targeted by the authorities because they suspect us of involvement with an armed group opposed to the government. My father was arrested in 1997, 2001, and 2005. After I finished secondary school, both my twin brother and I were arrested. Other family members were also arrested and tortured during 2005 and 2006. Between 2005 and 2006, I was arrested several times and forced to report weekly to an army camp.

In 2008, I left my hometown and went to the capital to try to find a job abroad. My father gave me the contact of someone who could help me get a visa and a job in Saudi Arabia. When I arrived, I could not reach this person. I stayed in a room arranged by my cousin and shared it with another man who was also planning to go abroad. I lent him my cell phone regularly. During my stay, I was away from the house at times, and the man used my phone.

Early in 2008, the police came to my residence in the capital while I was away. My landlady contacted me and told me that the police had arrested the man who had been using my phone and warned me not to return because the police were also looking for me. I moved to another house and stayed there until I left the country. I flew to Singapore, stayed there for eleven days, and then traveled to Malaysia, where I remained until 2009.

While I was in Malaysia, my mother informed me that my photograph had appeared in a newspaper in my home country, along with ten others, offering a reward for information about me. The article claimed I was involved in importing items for the armed group. After this, my twin brother was arrested, tortured, and questioned about my whereabouts.

On learning this, I applied for refugee status with the United Nations office in Malaysia and was accepted, but I was not given permanent status or allowed to work. I arranged through an agent to travel to Canada by ship. On September 5, 2009, I boarded the ship at sea and arrived in Canada in October 2009.

I fear returning to my home country because I have been publicly identified as a supporter of the armed group, my name and information have appeared in newspapers, and an international notice has been issued for me. If I return, I will be at risk of detention, interrogation, and torture.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a Tamil male from the Northern Province of my home country. In 1995, the army attacked my village, forcing my family and me to flee. We lived as internally displaced persons in a camp in another district, which was under the control of an armed group. In 1999, after another attack, we returned to our home, but in 2000, renewed violence forced us to move again to an area under army control, where I continued to live.

In 2007, the army and allied groups rounded up Tamils of a certain age group. I was arrested, interrogated, and my identity card was confiscated. I was released and told to collect my ID at the army camp the next day, which I did with my mother. In 2008, after a bomb exploded near my workplace, the army conducted a search and I was arrested again, but released later that day.

In 2009, when visiting relatives in a detention camp, the army suspected me of being connected to the armed group, confiscated my ID, and ordered me to report daily to the army camp. During these visits, I was sometimes interrogated and beaten. In 2010, I was told my daily reporting would end, but I must inform the army of any suspicious activity and report when ordered, or face the same fate as others who had disappeared. I feared I would be suspected of helping the armed group, as I had no information to give.

Shortly after, members of a pro-government group came to my home, demanded I work for them in an election campaign, and threatened me when I refused, believing I was connected to the armed group. I saw a white van near my home and went into hiding. The group returned to my parents’ home, demanding I report to their office. Fearing for my life, I left for the capital, obtained a passport and visa with help from my uncle and an agent, and stopped working. The group continued to threaten my family.

I left my home country in 2010, with the agent paying a bribe to the airport immigration officer. I boarded a ship and arrived in Canada in August 2010, where I claimed refugee protection.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I was born and raised in the capital city of my home country, where I lived my entire life until I left. I attended school for 16 years, including a year of university studies, and held several jobs since December 2000. I am single, and in 2002, I began living openly as a homosexual.

My problems started in 2000, when I was beaten by a group of homophobic students at my university. After this attack, I was advised to leave the country, so I went to the United States for five months and worked in Miami. I did not seek protection from authorities there because I believed they would not grant refugee protection based on sexual orientation, and I also experienced violence and discrimination in the United States. I returned to my home country and decided to live openly as a homosexual. My father drove me out of the family home because of his intolerance.

For the first time, I lived as part of a homosexual couple from 2002 to 2003. During that period, people from our neighbourhood attacked us twice, and I had to be hospitalized for three days after one of the attacks. After each attack, my partner and I went to the police, but they refused to listen to us and threatened to detain us for "immoral conduct." My partner and I separated in 2003. Later that year, I began another relationship, which lasted until mid-2003. We were attacked by homophobic individuals while walking hand in hand in a park. When we notified a police officer, he took us to the station and put us in a cell for a few hours for "immoral conduct." On another occasion, neighbours came to our home, attacked us, and told us to leave the neighbourhood. We had to be hospitalized again for a few days.

During this period, I lost my job twice. When I approached the ministry of labour, officials did not want to hear my case. Fearing for my life and unable to find protection, I left my country by plane in 2003, landing in New York the next day. I then travelled by road to the Canadian border, where I immediately expressed my intention to claim refugee protection. I fear that if I return to my home country, I will again be harassed and attacked by neighbours, students, and society at large, including the security forces. I do not believe the authorities in my country are able to provide me with adequate protection.

Testimony of Thomas Berg

My name is Thomas Berg. I am a member of the Roma ethnic minority in my home country. Throughout my life, I have faced constant harassment, discrimination, and insults from the majority population. Because of my ethnicity, I was treated as a second-class citizen. I tried to find work many times, starting at a young age, and would apply to five or six companies each year. Every time, as soon as they saw my name, I was refused employment and never hired.

To survive, I collected iron and bottles with members of my family. During these activities, we were often attacked by local people who would swear at us and throw rocks. We called the police several times to ask for protection, but instead of helping us, the police gave us tickets and laughed at us. My family and I tried different ways to protect ourselves, including moving from one city to another, hoping the situation would improve. However, the discrimination, harassment, insults, and beatings continued wherever we went.

In 2011, there were two specific incidents when my brother and I were attacked and beaten by aggressive locals. We reported these incidents to the police, but they did not intervene or offer us any protection. The lack of response from the authorities made us feel even more vulnerable and unprotected.

My family and I experienced repeated mistreatment over a long period of time. The cumulative effect of these incidents, combined with the lack of state protection and the ongoing discrimination against Roma people in all areas of life, led me to leave my home country. If I return, I will continue to face serious harm and will not be able to live safely or with dignity as a member of the Roma minority.

I tried to find work many times, starting at a young age, and would apply to five or six companies each year. Every time, as soon as they saw my name, I was refused employment and never hired.

My family and I tried different ways to protect ourselves, including moving from one city to another, hoping the situation would improve. In 2011, there were two specific incidents when my brother and I were attacked and beaten by aggressive locals. We reported these incidents to the police, but they did not intervene or offer us any protection. The lack of response from the authorities made us feel even more vulnerable and unprotected.

My family and I experienced repeated mistreatment over a long period of time. The cumulative effect of these incidents, combined with the lack of state protection and the ongoing discrimination against Roma people in all areas of life, led me to leave my home country. If I return, I will continue to face serious harm and will not be able to live safely or with dignity as a member of the Roma minority.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. I am a citizen of my home country and was a university student there. In 2002, I participated in demonstrations against the government, along with two friends. These demonstrations were in support of a university professor who had been imprisoned and sentenced to death. On two separate occasions in 2002, I joined these protests. During the first demonstration, when security forces arrived to break it up, my friends and I managed to escape in different directions. At the second demonstration, I was able to escape again, but my two friends were arrested by the authorities.

Two days after the second demonstration, security forces came to my home. I heard them arrive and escaped out the back of the house. My father was arrested instead and detained for two days. When he was released, he was ordered to report to the authorities once a week. The authorities told my father that I was considered an anti-revolutionary, active against the state and the religious leadership, and that I would be executed if found.

Fearing for my life, I decided to flee my home country. On a date in 2002, I left in a pickup truck that took me to a rowboat, which then took me to a cargo ship. The ship brought me to Dubai. In Dubai, I met someone who provided me with a French passport, and I flew to Malaysia. From Malaysia, using an Austrian passport, I flew to Japan. I stayed in Japan until 2003, when I was put on a plane to Toronto. Upon arrival in Canada, I claimed refugee protection. I fear that if I return to my home country, I will be arrested and executed because of my participation in anti-government demonstrations and my political opinions.

Testimony of Anna Larsen

My name is Anna Larsen. I am a woman from a state in my home country. In 2006, I was accused of an offence that is not considered a crime in most countries, and in many states of my home country, it is not prosecuted or is punished with probation or community service. On the day of my arrest, I was taken into custody by the sheriff’s department and charged. I was detained for several days, released, and then re-arrested and charged with additional counts. Throughout the criminal process, I was arrested multiple times and spent 13 days in jail.

The town where I lived is small, and the legal officials involved in my case had close relationships. The trial judge and the assistant state attorney had previously worked together, and the state attorney’s husband was also a judge in the same circuit. It was an election year, and both officials were in political positions, which affected my chances of fair treatment. I hired a lawyer and paid a large retainer, but he advised me to take a plea deal and did not refund my retainer. I complained to the bar association, but nothing happened. I hired another attorney, but he told me he could not afford to anger the trial judge because he had other cases before him.

I prepared for trial for two and a half years. The trial lasted three days, and I was found guilty. After the verdict, I was arrested again and spent more days in jail until my release pending sentencing. At the sentencing hearing, the state attorney recommended the maximum sentence, and the trial judge sentenced me to a lengthy jail term, running some sentences concurrently. I filed an appeal and spent more days in jail while my appeal bond was posted. My appeals to higher courts, including the Supreme Court of my state, were dismissed without substantive analysis of the sentence.

After the sentence, I decided that I would not get justice in the legal system of my home country, so I fled to Canada while my appeal was pending, contravening my bail conditions. I lived openly in Canada until I was detained by the authorities. I made a refugee claim and was released by the immigration division. I later learned that authorities in my home country issued a provisional warrant and made my case a priority. If I return to my home country, I face a prison sentence that is far more severe than what is typical for this offence, and I would have to serve at least 85% of the sentence before being eligible for parole.

Testimony of Peter Hansen

My name is Peter Hansen. After completing my studies in the United States, I returned to my home country and resumed my career as an educator in the field of vocational training. During my work, I witnessed illegal drug activities taking place at the school. Following the policy of the institution, I reported these activities to the administration, which then involved the police. The police investigation led to the identification of a gang involved in drug trafficking. Through an intermediary, I was warned that the gang knew I had instigated the police involvement. I was told that unless I ignored future drug activities at the school, I would be killed.

I reported these threats to the police, but they told me there was little they could do since it was my word against theirs. Shortly after, I was involved in a serious road accident with my vehicle, which ran off the road because unknown persons had loosened the lug nuts on the front tires. The police questioned a suspect, but he claimed he was not present on the island that day, and no further action was taken.

Fearing for my life, I requested and received a transfer in 2004 to another institution, where I served as an educator and administrator. In 2007, I observed a group of boys entering a vacant building on the school campus. Upon investigation, I discovered marijuana trafficking among students. I brought these students to the principal’s office, and the police were called. The source of the drugs was traced back to the same gang.

Within three weeks, I was alerted that two men were looking for me, and I learned that the gang leader had dispatched armed men to target me. I kept a low profile until the end of the academic year and decided to take my vacation in Canada to escape the threats. While in Canada, a friend informed me that my life was still in danger, as the gang believed I was responsible for recent police raids. Because of these ongoing threats, I decided to seek refugee protection in Canada.

My name is Cabdiraxmaan Hassan Nur. After completing my studies in the United States, I returned to my home country and resumed my career as an educator in the field of vocational training. During my work, I witnessed illegal drug activities taking place at the school. Following the policy of the institution, I reported these activities to the administration, which then involved the police. The police investigation led to the identification of a gang involved in drug trafficking. Through an intermediary, I was warned that the gang knew I had instigated the police involvement. I was told that unless I ignored future drug activities at the school, I would be killed.

I reported these threats to the police, but they told me there was little they could do since it was my word against theirs. Shortly after, I was involved in a serious road accident with my vehicle, which ran off the road because unknown persons had loosened the lug nuts on the front tires. The police questioned a suspect, but he claimed he was not present on the island that day, and no further action was taken.

Fearing for my life, I requested and received a transfer in 2004 to another institution, where I served as an educator and administrator. In 2007, I observed a group of boys entering a vacant building on the school campus. Upon investigation, I discovered marijuana trafficking among students. I brought these students to the principal’s office, and the police were called. The source of the drugs was traced back to the same gang.

Within three weeks, I was alerted that two men were looking for me, and I learned that the gang leader had dispatched armed men to target me. I kept a low profile until the end of the academic year and decided to take my vacation in Canada to escape the threats. While in Canada, a friend informed me that my life was still in danger, as the gang believed I was responsible for recent police raids. Because of these ongoing threats, I decided to seek refugee protection in Canada.
